This collection covers the first half of the mainline Mega Man X series, which is widely considered the best part. Mega Man X1 through X4 may not rank as my absolute favorites in the entire Mega Man franchise, but they’re all consistently fun.

The collection includes Rookie Hunter mode (basically easy mode), which is a great way for beginners to ease into the series without things getting too punishing, especially with how much damage enemies can deal. Being able to toggle this mode on or off is a nice touch, especially if you’ve already played these games on their normal difficulty and just want a more laid-back replay.

X1 is generally the fan favorite. While it’s not my personal number one, I’ll admit that in terms of its soundtrack, it’s probably the best overall.

X2 is fun, though the RNG-based, time-sensitive requirements to get the true ending can be annoying. It feels like a slightly less polished version of X1, but still worth playing.

X3 is a bit weird. Some parts are unnecessarily harder than they need to be, and the levels feel longer than X1 or X2. That said, it does have some cool weapons to mess around with, which keeps it interesting.

X4 introduces Zero as a fully playable character, and that alone makes it my favorite game in this collection. The usual Mega Man formula is great, but Zero fulfills my dream of a lightsaber-based 2D platformer. Adding boss power-ups tied to his saber abilities is awesome and makes replaying X4 with Zero so much fun. Plus, the infamous "What am I fighting for?!" meme from Zero’s voice acting is unforgettable.

Overall, the first half of the Mega Man X Legacy Collection is regarded as the best for a reason. While the series has its ups and downs, X1 through X4 are all strong entries and well worth playing.

Let me briefly say that I own the US version of this Steam product on a Windows 10 Operating system. I preordered both collections for myself on July 3rd with my own money. I was not given this for free to review.

Ok. On with the review.

First of all, I own all 8 X games in their original versions. I also own all of the original consoles they were released on. I also own Mega Man X Collection for both PS2 and GameCube. I've been playing these games for decades. I know what these games are supposed to play like on original hardware. I'm also a big emulator user as well. I've been using emulators since they first came out. I've also invested over $1,000 in a variety of hardware options to upscale and/or convert these retro games to HD on HDMI TVs using their original consoles. 

With that being said. I own a Windows 10 operating system on this PC. I've done a few tweaks to settings but nothing that should improve or hinder performance. All I did was download and installed a DirectX runtime from Microsoft, released in 2010. Then I went into Steam's Big Picture mode and changed some controller settings that are unique to that mode so my controller would be more compatible with this game. Also, FYI, apparently the controller settings that are exclusive to Steam's Big Picture mode also carry over when you play that game outside of Big Picture mode. Those settings solve a lot of controller problems that people have been experiencing with the Steam version.

Once I installed the DirectX runtime, I was able to get X Legacy Collection 1 to play audio. After I changed the settings in Steam's Big Picture mode, my controller was now compatible with the game and was giving me no more problems.

I've also noticed a bug with both collections where if you've already set either collection's screen mode to fullscreen, and you try to launch that collection, that collection's frame rate gets cut in half. To work around this... When you launch either collection and the frame rate is slow, go to the main screen and then select Options>Screen>Screen Mode and then change the mode to something other than fullscreen. Once you've change it, you can change it back and the frame rate will be normal again. However, that fix is only temporary. Because, if you quit either collection, and you had the screen mode set to fullscreen when you did so, you'll just run into the bug all over again when you re-launch that collection. At which point you just do the trick again to fix it. Or you can just have the screen mode permanently set to "Windowed" or "Windowed Full", since those modes don't seem to have this issue.

Outside of that. I tried to reproduce the problems that everyone has been complaining about. And I can tell you right now, I have 0% Input lag, virtually 0% slowdowns, and this is for all setting combinations. Yes. That's right. For Full Screen, Windowed, Windowed Full. And for all 3 different filter types with each of those modes. Even X1, X2, & X3's original slowdowns from the original SNES was improved. Not eliminated, but improved to the point where the original slowdowns are less noticeable.

Now before you think I'm some kind of lucky person, Think again. I own a $2,000+ desktop PC that I built myself. I've also got one of the more recent graphics cards installed from Nvidia. It's not the greatest one out there. But it's still pretty up there in performance.

I will be including links to articles (at the bottom of this review) that will help you if you are having the same problems that I had.

Now on to what I think of this collection.

I love the X series. This series is one of my all time favorite game series from any developer. In this collection, I love the fact that there is an option for different screen filter types, different screen aspect ratios, and different screen resolutions available in the settings. It really does give you a variety of ways to enjoy these classic games.

The extras are a nice touch as well. Lots of pictures, concept art, and a small collection of video trailers for the games from their original homeland of Japan. There are 1 or 2 English trailers featured as well.

As for the gameplay, I don't know what to say here since it plays exactly like the original games (depending on your controller). Everything is perfectly preserved gameplay wise.

There are 2 exceptions to this however.

In Megaman/Rockman X4's Intro, They removed a section of the video where General was reaching his hand out to salute his troops. I guess this was considered to offensive since you could look at it as a Hitler reference from Nazi Germany. I do not think this change was necessary since this edit was not made to any other release of this game in the past. Plus, by making this change, it slows down the pace of the entire video. And yes. The edit was made to both the Japanese and English version of this intro.

All Japanese songs have been replaced with the English music for all Rockman versions of each game. This includes all games. I'm guessing there was a licensing issue here, but only CAPCOM could answer this.

Outside of that, I love this collection. I love this collection a lot! If you are a fan of the X series or a fan of Mega Man as a whole, get this collection. It's fantastic. Just make sure you have a PC that can run the games at full speed.

I give this collection a 9 out of 10.

This collection of the first four Mega mans is great. The menus are well presented, very intuitive and fast to load.
I played the intro stage of each game and it works just fine as expected. The slowdowns that are present sometimes are proper from the Snes and it does not bother at all. Mega man X4 rans very good like it was in the PS1. The only issue i had in this game was some screen tearing when jumping and in the cutscenes on the X4 but i fix it in the nvidia control panel - manage 3D settings - program settings and set the vertical sync to FAST.

In X1, X2 and X3 you can save data in the same way as the original game by keeping the code that shows on screen. It does not bother me , you just take a picture or write down for when you want to load again your progress. In X4 you can save up to 6 different slots. 

I played with a wired Xbox One controller and i did not have issues with input lag.  You can set up in the case of the first 3 games the RB and LB buttons and in X4 you can use the triggers. The performance of the games is great. The FPS counter was always on 60 fps, and as i mentioned before the slowdowns are part of the emulation and they are not actual frame drop issues. Also i had no sound issues. 

The things that i liked from this collection are the menu options that you can access with the BACK button at any time where you can configure some main settings of the games such as monitor size, filter (i used type 1 because it gives a clean look of X), wallpaper (when you play in 4:3 so to fill the screen), Rookie Hunter Mode (increases the damage you make and lowers the damage you recieve) and to exit to the main title of the game or exit to the main menu of the collection. Also i liked the X challenge mode and the extra content that has such as trailers and galleries of photos.

One of the downsites i found was that you can only choose between 4 resolutions (1280x720, 1600x900, 1920x1080, 2560x1440). In my case i have full HD but this might be a big issuel if your monitor has a different resolution from the ones mentioned. 

Overall i give this collection a 9/10 and if you are Mega man fan as i am this collection is a must pick.

Personal ranking of games in this collection

X1- The Classic Megaman X game and arguably the best of the 16 bit games (imo)
X2- Improves several aspects from the first game such as having the dash by default however the level designs are not as good as the original.
X3- The weakest of the games in this collection. Little is improved over X2 and Zero while being playable is also limited in where he can be played plus nothing that happens in this game is really referenced in future games. 
X4- The best of the PS1 era of Megaman X games. Pick X or Zero at the start of your game and then play through the entire game only as them (X being the easier of the two while more story events tied to future games are mentioned in Zeros story)

Pros and Cons of the collection itself:

Pros:
Challenge mode where 2 bosses can be fought at once
several concept art and wallpaper unlockables for beating the games
can switch between the English or Japanese versions of each game

Cons: Controller input delay is commonly reported issue with the 16 bit games in the collection (experienced myself as well) 
No save state options (Not as big of a deal in later in the PS1 entries but the 16 bit games will make you redo entire stages if you game over instead of checkpoints

Verdict: Grab this collection on a sale if you want or have played any of the Megaman-X games listed

Mega Man X4 is such an awesome game. I played X1 and beat it years before X4, so I can say that X4 is definitely where new players can start. X4 is one of my favorite games nowadays because it's such a great game all around: Great Soundtrack, Great Bosses, Great levels, fair and good challenge (Except for General, screw him), and Zero is such a fantastic character to control. So powerful and rewarding to use. It's sad since when I beat the X4, and was sent back to the title screen, a smile visibly faded. That's how amazing X4 is. 

Oh, and it even includes Mega Man X1, X2, and X3 as bonuses, that's kinda cool.

Jokes aside, I feel like X4 should be your starting point if you want to get into Mega Man X. It does "getting newcomers into a series" right. Not jokingly easy or ridiculously hard, just right. 

Current issues addressed; I didn't run into input lag like many others do. Or even those odd crashes, perhaps I got lucky with the settings and build.  Maybe input lag DOES exist and I couldn't notice at all, but perhaps a person that played on OG hardware would know.

At least I can remap controls in the in game options, but I wished my layout would be saved so I wouldn't have to constantly visit the in game options menu every time. 

I got the good end of the stick, but apparently the bad side of it is rampant. Best to buy it on sale, test if there's input lag, try to fix, if not possible, then refund. Its NOT a bad collection, but I want to address the elephants in the room for safety. 

Beginners should start here, all things considered. There's even a "Rookie" mode if you're struggling too much.

For those experiencing slowdowns/input lag and screen tearing:

To workaround the slowdown issue go to the config.ini of the game and change the following section.

[CPU]
JobThread=15
RenderingThread=ON

For some idiotic unknown reason the default job thread is 7 but if you change it to 15 it will work just fine.

As a fervent admirer of the Mega Man X saga, my anticipation for the Mega Man X Legacy Collection was a blend of excitement and nostalgia. This collection serves as a treasure trove, rekindling the flames of yesteryears with its meticulously remastered classics. However, the decision to bifurcate the collection into separate entities puzzles me. Despite this, my affection for the series encourages me to embrace what we have been granted. After all, receiving this compilation is a boon we should wholeheartedly appreciate, surpassing the void of absence.

The X Challenge emerges as a standout feature, presenting an exhilarating test of mettle for aficionados of the X series. It’s a beautifully crafted ode to the enduring legacy of Mega Man X, challenging veterans and newcomers alike with a gauntlet that demands precision, strategy, and resilience. This mode alone makes the collection a must-have, offering a fresh and invigorating way to experience the franchise's rich lore and challenging gameplay.

Conversely, the inclusion of Rookie Hunter mode, designed ostensibly for achievement hunters, strikes a discordant note in the symphony of this collection. By rendering the player virtually invincible, it detracts from the essence of Mega Man X — a series celebrated for its challenging gameplay and intricate level design. While its intention to make the series more accessible is commendable, it feels somewhat misplaced in a compilation that should honor the rigorous challenge that defined these titles.

My journey with the Mega Man X Legacy Collection spanned across every console available, affirming my deep-seated love for these games. Each platform offered a unique lens through which to appreciate the painstaking effort invested into bringing these classics back to life. Yet, my unbridled admiration is tempered by the absence of Mega Man X5 from the collection. As the last entry that, in my eyes, embodied perfection, its omission is the sole reason this compilation falls just short of a perfect score.

Therefore, with a mixture of nostalgia, love, and a slight hint of longing for what could have been, I rate the Mega Man X Legacy Collection a 9/10. This score reflects not only the excellence contained within but also a yearning for the inclusion of X5 — the missing piece that would have completed this masterpiece. Regardless, this collection stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of the Mega Man X series, offering both a celebration of its past and a beacon of its timeless appeal.

I admit that I was skeptical about getting this one, given what people were reporting, but I had to see for myself.  To recap, the most common issues people are reporting are framerate drops, sound buffering issues, and control lag.  Enough people are reporting all three that I have no reason to doubt that they're experiencing those things on their given rigs.  On mine, however, I'm running into none of that.  So, for those with similar setups to mine, you're in luck.  Here's what I've got that'd be most likely relevant:

-Intel i7 2600K (not overclocked)
-24GB DDR3 RAM, PC3-12800
-nVidia GeForce GTX 1060 (6GB)
-Windows 10

Perhaps the issues are with AMD CPU and/or GPU?  In any case, with this setup, it works perfectly fine. Framerate is locked steady at 60FPS (I have VSync enabled, as I'm not a fan of screen tearing--if you want higher FPS, I'm sure it can deliver), sound isn't stuttering or distorted at any point, and perhaps most importantly, my XBox One gamepad is working just fine with no control lag.  Again, I have no doubt that the people reporting those issues are actually experiencing them, but with my rig, I'm not.  Hopefully Capcom will take note of which systems it is working for and which ones it isn't, and we'll see a patch or two for those having no joy so far.

All of that said...the games are as you'd expect, but ported to the PC.  You have some options on screen size and whether or not to apply a smoothing filter, as well as what window size/fullscreen/windowed fullscreen to use.  There are several additional features, like a Rookie Hunter mode for those new to Mega Man X, and some bonus features in the form of a mixed boss rush mode.  Overall, it's not bad at all--a good mix of a straight-up port with enough additional materials to make sure it stayed true to the source material while offering something new as well.

Mega Man X was actually the first Mega Man game I played - many years ago - but due to the high level of difficulty, I wasn't able to complete it.  The final boss, Sigma, has 2 forms and both can be challenging (near impossible) if you don't know his attack patterns or have all the items in the game to maximize your health and armor potential.  The final form, in fact, used 3/4 of my energy tanks as I tried to wear him down.   

There is a glitch in this port of the game's programming, which does not allow all 4 energy tanks to be used and I believe it's a problem found in most emulators according to net discussions I've read.

Mega Man X - as well as the rest of the Legacy collection follows the same flow as the previous Mega Man games. You are given an introductory stage to learn the controls.  You must fight 8 Robot Masters, steal their signature weapons, and then use those weapons against the individual robot masters in an order relative to which master is weak to which weapon.  Nothing has really changed from the original game's archetype except the presentation.

Graphics and Sound in the Mega Max X Legacy are typical of the SNES.  They are orchestral, heavy on bass and genuinely good to watch and listen to.  Many of the chip tunes are catchy and will stick with you even when the individual robot masters do not.  Many of them are rehashes of older robot masters from the classic NES games - only with superior graphics, sound and presentation. 

Mega Man X games have taken on a more Japanese "anime"-ish style and by the time you reach X8, you may feel visually overwhelmed. 

Control is tight across the legacy collection.  I was using an Xbox controller while the game was designed for an SNES controller.  

In Mega Man X, I found it impossible to do the Hadouken fireball using the D-pad, yet the analog stick made it easily repeatable- although - mildly awkward since I use the D-pad for movement rather than the analog stick. The D-pad was unresponsive when attempting this move. 

In Mega Man X2, I found it impossible to do the Dragon Punch without the joystick.  After grinding for an hour to get it, I completely neglected to use it in the boss rush or against Sigma. 

X3  has some very difficult bosses, stages and sections where you're forced to fight multiple bosses without being given much health recharge. The game has been precision engineered to be "hard".

X4 is colorful and a little less difficult than X3. I appreciate it when the "normal mode" is fair enough that you can beat individual stages using the default X-buster weapon. This may be my FAVORITE X game of the X franchise. It feels well balanced and the boss characters are memorable.  


The worst of the X games is arguably X7 (part of the Legacy Collection 2).  all the initial X games are good games - if not repetitive.  Each game has its own gimmicks. Some gimmicks appreciated while others aren't.  

I find playing through these games to be a nostalgia fix. Binge playing 30 YEARS worth of Mega Man titles in just a few months has basically ADDICTED ME to Mega Man. 

They are all "Nintendo Hard" - far more difficult than you'd expect games targeting kids to be. The amount of logic and muscle memory required to solve the challenges in the game would be IMPOSSIBLE without reading game magazines/help faqs or watching others play the game.  

If there's any true overarching criticism I have for these games, it's that they feel repetitive and unnecessarily difficult. But those two tropes defined the classic gaming eras - between 8 and 16 bit -  so in that respect, it's expected.

It's taken some technical finagling and driver upgrades, but yes, these games DO work! Your mileage may vary, as the other reviews have shown, but everyone has had different levels of success with various methods to get the games running steadily. In my case, getting the latest NVIDIA drivers and keeping the game running in windowed mode was all it took. Hopefully we can expect some stability patches soon, but in the meantime it DOES work and works fine!

Now for the games. This first collection, in particular, is filled with the classics. X1-4 are all great in their own right, for both casual players, speedrunners, and everyone in between. You can quickly switch between English and Japanese versions with the press of a button. Screen filters are there for anybody who wants them and they haven't impacted performance for me. You can remap controls, however trigger compatibility is missing in the SNES games as of this review. X1-3 also only have one save slot apiece, but X4 has its full save list as always.

The Museum is a great addition with loads of artwork, music, and photos of merchandise from over the years. The Day of Sigma anime from Maverick Hunter X is here as well! It's "HD" but hasn't exactly been rerendered, just upscaled from its original PSP release. Still a fun addition. In fact, all the videos have been upscaled, including the FMV's from X4, with drastically improved audio all around.

Speaking of audio, I have noticed many of the sound effects have been given a lot of extra kick from the original releases. They're the same, but remastered, and it's a welcome bit of polish.

Overall once you can get the games working they work just as you remember them. Yes, that includes the classic slowdown, which ideally gets patched into something like a "Fullspeed Mode" in the future. In the meantime this a great collection that no Mega Man X fan should miss! Hopefully we see a stability patch soon, and once we have that, everything should be smooth sailing.

At the very least, add this to your Wishlist so you don't forget about it!

[b]MEGA MAN X: 10/10[/b]
My first replay since the Gamecube's Anniversary Collection 14 years ago. MMX has maintained a spot in my top 5 games for over 20 years, and, putting my sad nerd goggles on, ties to one of my earliest bizarrely-specific childhood memories of my parents buying the SNES cart for my brother and me when I was 5 or 6. Gosh dang, we sank so many hours into this cart, so many replays and struggles against Sigma.

It's amazing that I *still* remember the placement of most of the enemies and secrets. That moment I paused in Sting Chameleon's page, just eyeing that pit and thinking "isn't that the one? but it's so close to the armor upgrade, they wouldn't put these right next to each other" while my fingers twitched, wanting to drop down. Or jumping off the cart at the start of Armadillo's stage to stock up on one-ups before I even see the iconic, out-of-place enemy. God, I love this game.

Perfect. So very, very, very perfect.

[b]MEGA MAN X2: 8.5/10[/b]
It's really hard to pinpoint why X2 just doesn't hold the same magic as the original. The bosses are (mostly) on par with the original 8; the X Hunters are a great addition; the number of awesome collectables and secrets just had me giddy. But also, like, it's just a bit bloated. Some of the levels are more of a drag than iconic. I don't think it's just nostalgia -- something is just slightly off with this sequel.

One thing it does really well -- for the standards of the time and the audience, at least -- is story. It builds a really suggestive, deep mythology with so little, and far beyond anything in the classic Mega Man series. I loved pouring over the robot designs and thinking of all the lost time between Mega Man and X -- and what all eventually transpired between Light and Wily, etc., as a kid. :)

[b]MEGA MAN X3: 7.5/10[/b]
MMX3 is still a solid game, and still features some of my favorite bosses of the series, but 2 big things really drag this game down as the worst of the early games:

- The collectathon baloney of X2 is doubled, and half of it is utterly pointless: The 4 robots are just...why? They have such limited uses, and the ways to unlock them are ridiculous. The Frog robit is the worst: On land, it's utterly useless, in the single water area where it can be used, it's...not as good as just being out of it, except to be used to find two other collectables hidden nearby. The super armor upgrades only prevent you from getting the ultimate armor down the road.

- The music. X2's music was good, but noticeably less memorable than the first. X3's music is just t e r r i b l e. Jarring, discordant...blah. I love the original's music dearly, but I never thought its being missing would affect my taste for the game so much.

The rest of the game is a mix of the best and mediocre of X and X2, meaning this game is still absolutely worth playing if you're a fan of the series. Neon Tiger and Blast Hornet are among the most fun mavericks of the series, imo. I love the degree of secrets and alternative routes towards Sigma that all affect the outcome in really obscure (perhaps *too* much so) ways.

[b]MEGA MAN X4: 8.5/10[/b]
Wow, this is a nostalgic trip back to the '90s for me. I didn't know so much of this game would have stuck with me compared to the first, but I must have played the heck out of it. The animation -- !! I forgot just how much this wow'd me despite not jumping onto the 3D bandwagon. X4's a bit of a return to form, somewhere between X and X2 in quality. Most of the collectable insanity is simplified and less reliant on backtracking.

The level design is more consistently superb a la the original, tho there are still a couple weird hiccups (Jet Stingray, Cyber Peacock). The bosses are -- except for Split Mushroom, who I just loathe for whatever reason -- among the best in the series...even if a little easy.

And holy beans, X4 is a walk in the park after the first 3 increasingly-difficult games. Boss patterns are a breeze -- even Sigma's.

Solid collection of four of the best action platformers ever made. X1 and X4 in particular are masterpieces. 

Pros:
- Four awesome games for 20 bucks is a pretty solid value. Even better when it gets a discount in a sale.
-Mega Man X4 has wicked fast loading times. Last time I played the game was the PS1 version and the difference between that and this version is night and day.
-Lots of neat little bonuses like artwork, old trailers, ability to play the Japanese version of each game.
-X Challenge seems kinda neat though I haven't really messed with it yet.

Neutral: 
-Emulation quality is serviceable. I've played X1 on a bunch of different emulators across a bunch of different platforms (Wii, Wii U, Raspberry Pi, PC, Tablet, etc etc) and this version isn't really much better or worse than any of those. I had an issue when playing X1 with an Xbox One d-pad where X would just stop in midair while dashing and it led to some very frustrating deaths but I can't be sure if that's this version of the game or just my controller going bad. 
-All the original slowdown from the OG versions is here. Some people prefer this for the "authentic" feel and others are annoyed because it's, well, slowdown. 

Cons:
-There's a bug where occasionally when I load the game, I just get a black screen and nothing happens. I have to manually open Task Manager to kill the process and upon restarting it usually boots. Not a huge issue but pretty annoying to keep dealing with. 
-No custom control bindings for X1-X3. I'd imagine this is especially frustrating for anyone playing this with a keyboard. 
-Even though it's all emulation there are no save states or rewinds. Most people will just bring in the proverbial "git gud" but it just seems like kind of lazy omission. Instead they offer you "Rookie Hunter mode" which essentially makes enemies do hilariously low amounts of damage to you. Between the two I'd much rather have save states.

Overall I think this is a really good value package for Mega Man X fans and prospective newcomers alike. If you're on the fence, maybe wait until a Steam sale if you can't spare 20 bucks. Also don't bother with X Legacy Collection 2 unless you're a Mega Man X diehard or a masochist, as the quality of the games in that bundle is significantly lower than this one. (Though I personally enjoyed X5, even though it did some pretty stupid stuff) If Capcom releases a fix for that black screen issue and adds custom control options for X1-X3, I'd honestly have no reservations about this collection. 

Oh and Capcom, if you could just add Maverick Hunter X as DLC that'd be greeeeaaat

Mega Man X Legacy Collection is a thoughtfully curated compilation that brings together the first four games of the iconic Mega Man X series, delivering a nostalgic yet polished experience that both longtime fans and newcomers can appreciate. Capcom’s decision to package these titles together not only preserves the core action-platforming gameplay that made the franchise a staple of the 16-bit era but also enhances it with modern conveniences, thoughtful extras, and quality-of-life improvements that make revisiting these classics a joy rather than a challenge.

From the moment you start the collection, it’s clear that Capcom put considerable care into maintaining the original feel of the games. Each title retains its tight, responsive controls, intricate level design, and memorable boss battles that defined the series. The progression through the games offers a satisfying sense of escalation, from the relatively straightforward stages and enemies of the first Mega Man X to the more complex environments and mechanics introduced in Mega Man X4. These games strike a near-perfect balance of challenge and fairness, rewarding skill and precision while encouraging exploration and experimentation with the series’ signature upgrade systems and weapon varieties.

One of the standout features of the Mega Man X Legacy Collection is the inclusion of a robust museum mode filled with concept art, character sketches, music tracks, and developer notes. This behind-the-scenes content provides a fascinating glimpse into the creation of the series and adds significant value for fans interested in the history and development of these games. The remastered soundtrack player is another highlight, allowing players to enjoy the classic chiptune compositions or switch to arranged versions, which breathe new life into familiar tunes while respecting their original spirit.

The collection also addresses some of the frustrations players might have encountered in the original releases. Features like save states, rewind functionality, and customizable controls are seamlessly integrated, allowing players to tailor the difficulty and experience to their preferences. These additions don’t dilute the core challenge but instead provide a safety net for those who want to enjoy the games without the frustration that often came with their original difficulty spikes. This approach makes the collection more accessible to modern audiences without alienating purists who want the authentic experience.

Visually, the games maintain their classic pixel-art style, which has aged remarkably well thanks to clean, colorful sprites and fluid animations. The transition to higher resolutions and widescreen displays is handled gracefully, preserving the sharpness and detail of the original artwork without distortion. The user interface is clean and unobtrusive, making navigation intuitive whether you’re jumping into a quick stage or delving into the extras menu.

While the collection focuses primarily on the first four titles, it does so with enough polish and attention to detail to feel complete. Fans of the series may miss the later Mega Man X games, but this set serves as a definitive look at the formative years of the franchise and showcases the evolution of its gameplay and design philosophy. It’s also a perfect entry point for new players curious about the roots of the Mega Man X series without the intimidation of the later, more complex entries.

In summary, Mega Man X Legacy Collection is a lovingly crafted anthology that respects the legacy of one of gaming’s most beloved franchises. It offers challenging, fast-paced platforming action wrapped in a package that honors the original games while modernizing them for today’s players. With its comprehensive extras, polished gameplay, and thoughtful quality-of-life features, this collection is an essential addition to any platformer fan’s library and a shining example of how to preserve and celebrate classic video games.

After a long hiatus, the X series makes a comeback to modern platforms packed with additional content, all 8 main games, and a Challenge mode that adds a lot of replayability and enjoyment both for seasoned players and newcomer alike.

There are a lot of things to consider, so I will be dividing my opinions on the game in two separate sections.

CONS: Let's get the bad things out of the way first. 
(Many people keep mentioning that the game constantly crashes, boots up to a black screen, doesn't register inputs and is full of glitches and errors here and there. I've played for more than 10 hours and this has not happened to me even once. Game has worked perfectly fine and smooth, so I can't complain about that)

- As expected, the games are emulations. Many of the performance issues that were present on the original games (both for the SNES and PlayStation consoles) are still present. You will experience lag and slowdowns on specific sections where a lot of enemies congregate, for example. This affects the pacing of the game and is something that should have been revised.
- To try and create the illusion of high definition and remastered character sprites, the game offers the player the use of filters. The HD filter, however, makes spirtes look unpolished and ugly. They could have done a better job with this. A missed opportunity to refresh the look of the classic X games.
- Mega Man X4 features animated cutscenes that look awful by today standards, not because of the animation, but the resolution. They could have remastered these cutscenes to look way better than what they do.
- The SNES games have limited controller customization options. To keep it as close as possible to the SNES controller (which only has 2 shoulder buttons instead of the modern 4 button standard) they take away the option of using trigger buttons, which is a real problem.
- The 4 games featured in this collection do not have additional content. All the additional content was poured in the collection itself, so you will only be able to access to it on the main menu. They didn't even include remastered tracks or remixes for stages or boss battles. The rest of the music is accessible through the Music Player option, but it automatically pauses when you switch windows, making it useless as a background tune while you work on something else.

PROS: Now let's talk about all the things this collection gets right.

- You can freely change between the US and JP versions freely, and have two separate save-files for you to play without compromising your current one. Having this option available for Mega Man X4 is great because you can enjoy the cutscenes with japanese voice acting which is infinitely better than the american dub.
- Additional content includes character scans, concept art, early designs of characters, cover arts, alternative covers, wallpapers, a music player with music from the entire collection, The Day of Sigma OVA, collectables, and tons of information regarding the Maverick Hunters, Mavericks, character traits and motivations, lore and much more. Valuable stuff if you are a Mega Man X fanatic and want to have an entire database all together in the same place.
- Achievements add a ton of replayability. You probably have a favorite X game from the bunch (mine being Mega Man X4) that you can probably beat in less than an hour and that you have memorized from top to bottom. The game now rewards you for that, but also motivates you to try less usual paths and boss strategies which helps you enjoy the games you have played for countless times in a new, completely different way.
- Challenge mode tests your knowledge of the games and your abilities as a Maverick Hunter. This is the best way of giving seasoned Mega Man X players their money's worth. Now that you have beaten all the Mavericks from X to X6, you will have to beat two of them at the same time, while only being able to bring 3 weapons from a pre-selected bunch with you. Your knowledge of enemy patterns, weaknesses and resistances will be very valuable to be successful in this mode. Also, it comes with Online Leaderboards to check how good you are against other players globally.

To conclude, this Collection will allow you to enjoy what is, debatable, the better half of the Mega Man X franchise. If you have never experienced the games before, this is a great way of enjoying them for the first time. If you have beaten all the games before, Achievements and the X Challenge mode will keep you busy and entertained enough that you will feel like you actually bought the X Challenge mode with the 4 games bundled as a gift for your purchase.

It's a nice convenience to have this collection, if you're like me and mostly play on Steam these days -- and if you don't really feel like busting out old consoles or mucking around with emulators.

That having been said, this collection isn't the best - but there's still some good stuff in here.

[b]Input lag[/b]: This isn't a proper PC port, but rather a collection of poorly-emulated ROMs with a shiny UI. There is a noticeable input latency delay of at least a few frames, particularly in X1 - though it's also present in X2 and X3. On the flipside, X4 felt fine to me. The games are still playable, and I didn't have any problem getting all the Steam achievements, but it's a somewhat sluggish experience. Any kind of speedrunning here is definitely a no-go, as the latency issue is apparent even in casual play (such as when you're trying to climb up a wall quickly). 

I run a higher-end PC setup (a watercooled 5950x + 3090) so I don't agree with those who say this issue only exists for people running potato-tier PCs. It's a problem that can be alleviated somewhat by removing screen filters or turning off vsync, but it's not a full fix. If you don't notice the delay, great. But... it's there. If performance is important to you, you're still better off with the original console versions or emulating these games yourself.

[b]In-game Lag[/b]: This collection emulates the SNES versions of the games for X1-X3, which means certain bits of in-game lag are preserved as well (such as the final minecart section in the Armored Armadillo stage). If you prefer the lag for nostalgic reasons, then this is all fine and well - but it makes me wonder why they didn't opt for the newer revisions, like the ones included in the Mega Man X Collection on the GCN/PS2 where this in-game lag was addressed for the most part. 

[b]Versioning[/b]: I was excited at first to see that there was an in-game option to switch between game editions (Mega Man X vs. Rockman X), so I started up Rockman X4 expecting to see the intro video with [i]Makenai Ai Ga Kitto Aru[/i], and yet... the generic NA music started playing over the Rockman X4 video. The scene with the General's salute has also been censored out. While the Rockman editions do have Japanese cutscenes + text (as well as other expected changes like Cyber Peacock -> Cyber Kujacker), the absence of the music is a letdown. Thankfully, the cutscenes are just .wmv files that can be swapped at will, and there are some Steam guides you can look up to help point you in the right direction. So with a little modification, you can get the experience you want - but at this point you have to wonder why you're buying something just to swap out a good chunk of its content. I also wish they went with the PS version of X3 like they did before, since that comes with additional videos/music not present in the SNES version here. 

[b]Extras[/b]: There is a section of the menu containing a media collection full of original artwork, concept art, Japanese MMX trailers, pictures of apparel, trading cards, action figures, etc. While all of this content is free to look up on Google and YT, it's all neatly organized in one place here. It's a pretty cool feature, and probably one of the highlights of this collection, but it's not something you'll spend a lot of time on.

[b]X Challenge Mode[/b]: The challenge mode is probably the best part of this whole thing. There are multiple stages, 9 in total. In each stage, you choose up to 3 weapons from a small pool of options. Then you have three battles. In each battle, you fight two different Mavericks at the same time. So there's a bit of a strategic element, since you only have 3 weapons to use against 6 Mavericks. You have to prioritize what weapons you think will give you the most bang for your buck. You also have to be careful in how you fight, as some bosses have more advanced attacks when their health drops low enough - which means you may want to completely destroy one boss first. Easy Mode is just "spam to win" and is nothing special - though you have to beat it to unlock Hard Mode, which is where the magic happens. On Hard Mode, you have to actually be careful and know how to deal with two boss patterns simultaneously. Some pairings are pretty tricky, where the strength of one boss can compensate for the weakness of another. The one criticism I have, however, is that many bosses from the MMX series never get utilized here at all, while others show up multiple times. 

[b]Steam Achievements[/b]: Most of the achievements (which also double as in-game "medals") are things you've already done countless times in these games, such as completing them, firing all the weapons, finding all the collectibles and armor upgrades, and so on. Some challenges are a little different - namely things like completing Magna Centipede's stage without getting caught by the searchlights. Which is... actually kind of tricky, haha. It's not something I ever paid attention to before, so it took me a few tries. But the achievements are a nice way to help you do everything there is to do in these games, in case you never really bothered before.

[b]Saving[/b]: No savestates unfortunately. You have the usual password system, with an additional single-save/load feature. It's basically equivalent to having the game memorize a password for you so you don't have to enter it yourself. 

Overall... this collection is a mixed bag. Many diehard fans will probably enjoy it anyway, despite its faults - I know I did. Others will find the input latency issue to be a dealbreaker. This is one of those games where I wish I could pick a "Mixed" rating, but I'm erring on the side of a thumbs up because I still had fun.

X Challenge Mode is cool, but it's not worth $20 if that's all you're buying it for (wait for a sale in this case). Otherwise I'd say buy it if you like the convenience of having the games on Steam, or if you like Steam achievements, or even if you just want to support the franchise.

So far, so good!  Solid entry in the Mega Man PC release line-up.

Good:

-Games play fairly identically to original hardware; MMX4 is super snappy, almost no loadtimes
-Low-end frequency tweaks to MMX1-3.  More bass, more brutal bangers, great move
-No input lag!  Even with a wireless controller, games feel SUPER responsive, only took six dashing jumps to get arm upgrade in MMX1, tying my previous record on a SuFami
-1440p scaling is good!  Everything looks great
-Museum includes promotional trailers for each game; check out the Rockman X promo for some beta footage!
-MMX ON PC
-No option for MMX3 Saturn soundtrack.  Yes, this is absolutely plus for me.  Those arrangements were atrocious.

Eh:
-MMX 1-3 do suffer from very occasional frame jitters/skips.  Very infrequent however.
-No save states, but they do save passwords
-MMX4 screen options 1 and 2 are identical, no option for original scaling
-Full screen veritcal aspect stretch isn't using integer scaling so you'll see some inconsistent pixel allignment in the best available video output option
-No options to try out bosses in Museum mode like you could in MMLC2
-Capcom USA must not have kept their trailers on file; most of the early entries only have Japanese promos available

Poor form:
-No customizable controls, probably frustrates keyboard enthusiasts

Final notes:  It's 2018, frankly it's time for people to spend $15 on a used wired 360 controller (You've been complaining since Castlevania!) so the only huge negative for me's fairly inconsequential, but I wouldn't argue if it came up at some point.  Plays great with an Xbox One wireless controller, 1440p looks sharp as heck.  Love the interface.  Love the games!  Mega Man X4 is all hu-ha-hoh, it's not over yet (as it should be).  I think the lack of save states may have been an artistic call; save-scumming is a cop-out.  Git gud!

Maybe this is a "My Rig Versus Their Rig" issue (My PC's pretty buff) but... I'm thinking people are mistaking the "lag" with how the game performs normally possibly?  Everything I tried felt fairly identical to actual hardware performance (maybe even a bit better in spots, but that's possibly my mind playing tricks on me).  MMX2 and 3 chug often, and yes, even MMX lags at times, even on a SNES.  Emulation performance is about a step below Higan, but honestly I even get frame hitches in that so it's not MUCH worse.  Capcom has released much worse.

I'm somewhat of a snob when it comes to MMX emulation, and honestly, these perform admirably across the board, and a huge nod to boosting the bass in the original three titles, really helps drive the awesome tunes.  Speaking of which, while people hoist the MMX PS2 collection in their arguments in performance (much of the lag inherent in the original titles is greatly reduced), they fall strangely silent on how NONE OF THE MUSIC in the SNES titles actually loops properly; they have a fade-out and repeat, it's absolutely gross. This is a huge drawback for X3 since the PC/PSX version of it featured animated cut scenes and improved music (they even included 2 music tracks of the PSX version in the musuem), which I personally prefer for the most part (especially Dr.Lights theme, the SNES version of it is just horrible). Since this is a collection of 4 games, I'm going to split this review into a review of each one, plus the X Challenge.

X1: As the game that placed the X series on the map, the first game in the series is, quite simply, a masterpiece. While rough around some edges, the never truly felt unfair or made me feel like I was "cheated" in any way.

X2: A fantastic sequel to a fantastic game. The armor upgrades are fun, the weapons are useful, and the final boss, while easier than the first game's, is still a solid challenge.

X3: This is when the series started to suffer in the quality department. The levels here suffer from "Surprise bitch" moments when it comes to enemy placement, and the chip system I believe could have been handled much better. And of course there's Zero, who played just like X with no real significant changes.

X4: This is the game that X3 should have been. At least in how Zero is played. An awesome game with fun levels and even more fun weapons. Zero's techniques are by themselves worth the replay, just to play around with combos.

X Challenge: The new thing in the collection. A dual boss rush. It's as simple as that. Three rounds of dual boss fights. You can either fight against them with just your X-Buster or fight them holding 3 boss weapons from a list. The fights range from simple, to challenging, to fucking frustrating. And while that is true, I never felt like the challenges were unfair.

The megaman X series has always been a classic. Growing up with these game is an unforgetable experiences. The characters, the gameplay and the background music make it worth wild. There will be no regrets playing this game.

I still don't get why they bothered making two separate collections for the X games, especially because XLC2 is the definition of sloppy seconds, but as for XLC1, it's the most convenient way to have the best of the X series on demand whenever you want. Reviewing the things that it adds... Basically nothing of value. Being able to play the great OSTs is nice, being able to swap over to the Japanese versions for whatever reason is neato, X Challenge is a hit-or-miss addition, but X's armor in X Challenge also looks ghetto as can be; it literally looks like someone went ham with the paint bucket tool in MS Paint. The balancing is also... questionable at times. Anyway, that's all I can muster for the additions. Moving on to the actual games, they're all here and accounted for, but with some major and minor issues. The biggest one, and I have no idea what genius thought this was a stellar idea, is that when playing X1, X2 and X3, you have to rebind your controls every time you boot up the games, which is insanely annoying, especially since there's no way to actually rebind them in-game, meaning you have to restart the game and rebind them from the main menu. Yeah, it's not that big of a deal  and only takes a few seconds, but why is it here to begin with? The save function is also janky, since the people working on this collection either couldn't be bothered to make a save feature or were just plain incompetent, so instead of an actual save feature, it instead just reloads a corresponding password. Even the checkpoint save system in MMLC2 would have been superior. At least then, you wouldn't have to remap your controls every single time you want to play the games. As for the input lag that people keep reporting, I personally haven't experience it, so I can't really say much on that front. I also don't get why the PS1/Sega Saturn versions of X3 and X4 respectively aren't available. You're telling me I can play the original Rock Man versions of the games, but not the other ports, that in some aspects are superior to the SNES/PS1 counterparts? Why? I also don't remember if the slowdown from the SNES games is present in XLC1, mainly because I'm too lazy to go and check it. If it hasn't been fixed, then you're basically just getting a worse experience than emulating. As for the actual games themselves, as I've stated before they're the best in the X series by far, however; they've still got a few flaws as far as game design goes.

X1 Section: 

«Pros»
- 'Tis a Mega Man game, therefore; it controls well, except for the dash sometimes. This applies to all the games in the X series. (Except for X6 and X7.)
- The soundtrack is godly.
- The boss fights can be pretty enjoyable once you know what you're doing.
- Gives X the gift from the gods of not getting screwed from knockback while in midair over pits.  
- Generally fun just to mindlessly mash the shoot, dash and jump buttons.
- A fair number of unlockables and collectibles. 
- Replay value that's through the roof.

«Cons» 
- Intro Stage is slow and boring on repeat playthroughs due to lack of being able to dash.
- Literally every collectible requires the dash, either directly or indirectly, in order to be obtained.
- Not having the dash makes beating the bosses a pipe dream.
- Dash can be finicky compared to X2/X3.
- Level design's a bit lackluster.
- Weapons break the bosses hardcore.
- Literally just pick Chill Penguin as your starting Maverick; anyone will just result in a brutal difficulty spike.

X2 Section:
«Pros»
- Generally the most well-designed out of the SNES games as far as game design theory is considered.
- Doesn't suffer from the issue of 7/8 bosses and basically all of the unlockables requiring the dash.
- Bosses are generally fun, enjoyable and more well-balanced, albeit a bit easy.
- Level design is much cleaner with a stronger emphasis on platforming than X1.
- Dash controls better here than in X1.
- Backtracking for stuff isn't that common.

«Cons»
- OST is pretty meh for Mega Man standards.

Note: There's not really much to say regarding X2; it's just a solid game and sequel. Pretty much all of the pros mentioned in X1 also apply for X2, X3 and X4.

X3 Section:
«Pros»
- Probably the hardest game out of the collection, if that's your kink.
- The largest amount of collectibles in the collection, which by extension gives it the most replay value.
- Weapons are the best in the collection and are much more well-balanced than in X1, X2 and X4. X2's and X4's weapons were meh. Not terrible, but not really something most players would be actively trying to experiment with, and X1's were outshined by the Storm Tornado and Fire Wave.
- Music is better than X2, though it might be a bit of an acquired taste. Might be a con if you're not into gritty grunge rock.

«Cons»
- My god, that early game difficulty spike will spear your rectum hard if you're not prepared. X3 is easily the most unforgiving out of the collection, and probably the entire series, save for like, X6.
- The bosses feel a bit weaker in terms of balancing and game design. Certainly not in power, as they can kill default X in like 3 hits, have patterns that are hard to get the hang of, or are just complete dumpster fires without abusing their AI with their weakness.
- Zero's implementation sucks hard and is basically useless; just play X4 if you want Zero action.
- For some reason, they fixed the issue of enhancement chips not being interchangeable in the PS1 version of X3, but not in the SNES version, so... sucks to suck, I guess.
- The backtracking in this game is aids if you pick a bad order, which is very likely, since there's only, like, one good order to playthrough the game.
- Starting from X3 is when Mega Man games start to... struggle a bit with visibility, especially when verticality is a factor, so have fun occasionally facehumping spikes, bottomless pits or enemies that shave off a clean 3rd of your health in the early game. 

X4 Section:
«Pros»
- Easily the most competent level design, boss design and general game design theory of the collection.
- Slowdown doesn't exist natively; experience may vary if you're running it on a literal potato. 
- OST is pretty nice with a wide array of tunes with great instrumentation and composition, however; since the PS1 version doesn't loop tracks seamlessly like the Saturn port, the music just starts and ends abruptly. I don't remember if this is an issue in XLC1, because I'm too lazy to go check.
- Controls are the best in the collection.
- Zero enjoys his promotion to fully playable character with a unique and customized playstyle that's pretty fun.
- Voice acting is so bad that's good.
- Sound design is great.
- The animation and pixel art in general hold up really nicely and look amazing.
- Bosses are insanely fun to run through as Default X and Zero, though problems will be discussed in the cons section.
- Has innate functionality for saving. Thank the lord.

«Cons»
- Probably the easiest X Game.
- Level Design is nice to burn through and speedrun, however; the levels feel short and don't offer much in the way of challenge.
- Checkpoint system could be seen as too generous, allowing for mindless brute forcing. It's so bad in some stages that you can literally walk the level, accept all of the hits and still progress because of the checkpoint. When you die, everything gets refilled, and game overs send you back to the last checkpoint anyway. I really don't get why lives are still a thing in this game.
- The bosses with the weaknesses turn into absolute pussies.
- Story sucks, even by Mega Man standards.
- Collectibles are lowered from X3.

Tl;dr: The only real pro is accessibility.

Mega Man X Legacy Collection (Vol. 1) is definitely a fine addition to the MMLC Series adding the X-Series (Vol.1 inclues X1-X4) to the Legacy Collection lineup. However, a few shortcomings with the collection itself holds it back meeting the expectations the the Classic Mega Man Legacy Collections had set. Some of these include:

[b] Custom Controls and Controller Support [/b]
A main annoyance, although only purely affecting quality of life, is the inability to save custom control schemes between sessions. The triggers must also be used rather than the bumpers for X1-X3, also another quality of life item. This was quite suprising as the Classic MMLC (CMMLC) saves control schemes between sessions as well as making quite accessible in the Main Options before entering any game.

[b] Input Lag [/b] (partially me whining cause I suck.)
A major gripe with the MMXLC is the is noteable input lag, for me the issue was mostly in X1 and X4 and whilst X2 and X3 had some is wasn't as noticable as the other two titles. This significantly effects the gameplay of the collection as many platforming sections that require precision were made much harder than they should have been. [spoiler] X1: Sigma's Fortess 1 and X2: X-Hunter Stage 2 are repeat offenders. [/spoiler]

[b] Gave Saves [/b]
In contrast to the Classic Mega Man Legacy Collection, MMXLC makes use of the password systems from the original games to save and store progress made. This comes with minor impacts on gameplay in the final stages as progess though final stages and secret weapons, [spoiler] Hadoken and Shoryuken [/spoiler] , are not saved in the password system and must be recompleted/reobtained. This is a large change from the CMMLC allowing the player save in any location, though being quite cheesey acting as a 'save state' it brought alot of flexability to saving progess. MMXLC does supplement the 'save states' with a less forgiving Rookie Hunter Mode to a degree but misses out on the flexability of progess saving system of CMMLC.

[b] Faithful Repoduction? [/b]
The MMXLC does a very nice job of emulating the X-Series including alot of the quirks and gimmicks imposed by the limits of the original systems (SNES and PS1). However, this leads to uncomfortable and sometimes unwanted time periods where the game would slow to a snails-pace during combat or having a large amount of entities on screen. MMXLC also stays faithful to many iconic quirks I've associated with the series growing up like the the cutting of background tracks to make way for other SFX. An option to toggle these would be quite nice.

Overall, the Mega Man X Legacy Collection, dispite its flaws, brings new life to the X-Series with the inclusion of Rookie Hunter mode for people new to the Mega Man franhcise and X Challenge for the veterans and long-time Megaman X fans. After some tweaking to how the games run and perform on less limiting systems such as PC and other consoles. Shortcomings aside, Mega Man X Legacy Collection definitely haas the potential to be a stellar nostalgic hit but is not quite complete though I still recommend it to newcomers or verterans to the X-Series alike whether it be a physical or digital copy of the game.

Other Notes: Review does not cover MMXLC Vol. 2 and X-Challenga Game Mode.

I’m surprised it has taken so long for Mega Man X to make its way to Steam, fans have been screaming out for years that they want it available on Steam. A.R.E.S came very close, but left everyone wanting more. 20xx had the gameplay, but some of its procedural stage designs became spike traps. Mighty #9’s hype train ultimately left the game not living up to expectations. Capcom has finally realized that there is a market for their older games and ported the first four of the X series together in one collection, 25 years after the original games release. If you like any of the X series (or the above mentioned games) or like great gaming soundtracks then you owe it to yourself to pick up the first collection.

You play as X (an Android) as he has to go between different stages and destroy the Reploids masters (Replica Android’s that are based off X’s design) that have gone maverick and are threatening humanity. X knows most of the master’s in each game, and being a pacifist at heart who has to fight his former friends makes his struggles that much harder. Each master has a weakness to one of the other masters weapons, and the path through each game is decided heavily on this. Each stage contains lots of secrets from upgrades that increase your life to part upgrades that make grant you new abilities. Each x game progresses this concept a little further, with the dash becoming more distinctive and the buster upgrades allowing bigger blasts to eventually have two variants in X4 to choose from.

I think the production quality on X -X3 was very high, the stages are designed very well, the music is phenomenal and encourage exploring and trying different things to succeed. The boss designs were great and certain weapons removed abilities from other bosses. X2 and X3 allowed different outcomes depending on your actions during the game. X4 was the shift from Super Nintendo to PlayStation and it shows. The graphics aren’t quite as crisp (there is a lot more animation however for every enemy and X/Zero), and my god the added voice work is horrible. YouTube any of the movie scenes, they are very low quality for a AAA game. It did add a host of new features like hover cycle stages, rotating stages, a energy weapon sub tank and 2 separate storyline’s. X4 seems a lot shorter, but is essentially 2 games, one where you play with X, and the other you play with the swordsman Zero. Abilities are different between the 2 as are the playstyles (Zero comes fully upgraded with parts already) and most of the upgrades from bosses are enhanced abilities rather than moves.

If you were a fan of the soundtracks from the originals then there is a built in music player where you can load up the tracks from the first 4 games and play, though if you want to play them outside the game you are forced to pay the stupidly high DLC prices for them. One game soundtrack costs more than the collection!

I wouldn’t bother playing the game on a keyboard, it was designed for a controller. Make sure you have one you want to have a good time playing this.

As a port Capcom have out done their selves, adding tons of extras and different modes for you to explore. I don’t think there has been a port as comprehensive as this. All games allow you to play in a rookie mode, which drastically reduces the damage you take. There is a challenge mode where you fight 2 bosses at the same time (from all the games x through to x6) and have to select which weapons to use before to compete in a global leaderboard. You can view tons of artwork, listen to the soundtracks and see all of the merchandise and old TV ads. There is a prequel animation that explains the events before the first game, it was interesting to watch as I hadn’t seen it before. You have the option to stretch the aspect ratio (the games where produced when widescreens didn’t exist) or keep the original and full the boarders with artwork, as well as adding different visual filters to the game in case you want that authentic CRT monitor or old TV feel. My one gripe is that in some stages the game slows right down for no reason, for games that were made in 93 this shouldn’t be a problem in modern hardware.

If you are chasing 100% achievements then it’s quite possible, as finishing all the games isn’t overly difficult, and everything else should either come naturally during gameplay or doesn’t take long to find.

The Mega Man X series has always been my favorite series in the Mega Man franchise, and having all the Mega Man X games, from X1-X8 in a convenient, modern package is perfect. (Because oh my goodness, good luck buying physical copies of the original games, especially X2 and X3)

The visual filters are hit and miss (under NO circumstance should you choose the "smooth" filter, it just looks wrong, I recommend the CRT filter), and the choice of wallpapers are a bit inconsistent (I suggest using the X Challenge for a wallpaper/border that can work across all games), but of course, the real star of the show are, the games.

Legacy Collection 1 offers Mega Man X1-X4, and they are all fantastic games (with X4 being my favorite, and X3 being, well, X3), and it is worth mentioning that the version of Mega Man X3 in this collection is based off the original SNES release, and not the enhanced PS1 release with an arranged soundtrack and FMVs (the PS1 version of X3 can be found in the 2005 Mega Man X Collection). The addition of the Rookie Hunter mode does help new players ease into the game, but in several instances, Rookie Hunter mode makes the game a little TOO easy, but since it can be turned off on a whim, it's great for those who want to switch the game to the intended challenge, which offers the best of both worlds.
Oh, and for all you achievement hunters out there, this game offers some pretty challenging achievements, it even taught me elements of some of the games that I never knew about!

And then we have X Challenge, where you square off with two Mavericks at once, and some of the combinations you fight are just the stuff of nightmares...This mode is just a novelty (and achievement fodder), and nothing more.
The icing on the cake with this collection is the extensive art gallery and music player for each game, as well as a detailed catalog of any and all Mega Man X related merchandise, which is a very interesting look for those who are curious.

If you're a Mega Man X fan, or a Mega Man fan in general and have wanted to get into the X series, this collection has definitely the best way to jump in!

Let me preface this review by saying that, as of the date of this review's publication, this collection is unfortunately plagued by several technical issues ranging from random crashes at the bootup screen to low FPS or input delay on rigs that far outranks the recommended specs. Personally, I've only experienced random crashes at startup on my custom-built gaming PC (i7 quad-core CPU, dual GTX 860M SLI GPU), but as of right now, buy the Steam version at your own risk. Now, on to the review of the individual titles you get in this package:

Mega Man X easily makes a strong case for being one of those games that reaches sheer perfection, the fast and dynamic,  ever-evolving gameplay that greatly rewards exploration and experimentation in ways the classic series had only flirted with, the rocking soundtrack without a single forgettable track in its entire library, the perfect difficulty that stays engaging without disuading players from trying new tactics... It's something truly special. 

The sequel knew what worked and stayed its course while adding an exciting twist of unpredictability to every playthrough through the X-hunter system, ensuring that no two playthroughs played out quite the same, resulting in no less than four optional boss fights, all leading up to the series' first two separate endings. 

X3, while introducing promising concepts, such as the ability to play as everyone's favorite SA-rank hunter Zero and the expanded ride armor system, unfortunately fell short of expectations for many thanks to its rather simplistic level design, overly punishing enemy design, the underutilization of the previously-mentioned Zero and ride armor mechanics along with a repetitive soundtrack. One thing the game does succeed at is providing a slightly tougher level of difficulty than your average X game, which makes it fill quite a nice niche for those who've played through the original two SNES classics over and over and are looking for something a bit more challenging in the same style. Though this slower, more methodical take on the X series is certainly an aquired taste compared to its speedier counterparts. It is also worth noting that the version of X3 featured in this collection is the SNES original rather than the PS1, Saturn and PC port that featured CD-quality music and animated cutscenes.

X4, at first glance primarily goes for a safer approach than any other X game by simply sticking to the standard Mega Man game progression structure without any real experimentation in terms of mechanics thrown into the mix. This is only from X's perspective though, as X4 finally introduces Zero as a full-time playable character with an entirely unique close-range and mobility-oriented fighting style that is completely unlike anything else seen from the franchise up to this point, and it works out wonderfully despite the radical shift in gameplay structure. The crisp 2D visuals that haven't aged a day are just icing on the cake.

Of course, the core games aren't all the gameplay you're getting here. As trailers made sure to highlight, there is also the X Challenge mode: A one-on-two boss rush bonanza wherein you suit up in a visually overhauled but functionally identical version of the nerfed fourth armor from X5 to take down a wide variety of X's 2D adversaries. You start off with two lives and get to choose between a handful of special weapons and then gets sent on your way to take on three matches back to back with no break or healing inbetween. The first two matches will be identical in both versions of the Legacy Collection but the third will be unique.
There's so much more content than just the already excellent games. This Collection is well worth the money even at full price.

“The Original Mega Man series is one of the best series of games ever” Hold on, I’m going to have to pull a Kanye here. “Mega Man X is one of the best Mega Man games of all time.” Thank you.

The fact is when the original Mega Man Legacy Collection came out, I picked it up and played it, and it was a solid game. However, even with save states and more, the entire time I played it, I kept thinking “I really miss Mega Man X”. So Mega Man Legacy Collection 2 came out and admittedly I haven’t played it yet, but I still wanted the Mega Man X versions. Finally, Capcom figured it out and released Mega Man X Legacy Collection. This is a collection I’ve been dying to play, even playing it as one of the first games I tried at E3 this year. So was I wearing nostalgia goggles or is Mega Man X Legacy Collection live up to the hype?

Well, the good news is that yes, Mega Man X Legacy Collection has the best games of the series in it. Since I’m reviewing the games on Steam, I am lucky enough to actually have gotten Mega Man X Legacy Collection and Mega Man X Legacy Collection 2 as separate games. The good news here is that I can review them at different times. The better news is I’m reviewing ONLY the Mega Man Legacy Collection here. Which means this review only concerns itself with Mega Man X, Mega Man X2, Mega Man X3, Mega Man X4 as well as the all-new Mega Man X Challenge.

Why is that good? I get to talk about four amazing titles and not a certain other title starring a new character that is called X7. With that foreshadowing out of the way, we can talk about the Mega Man X Legacy Collection.

The fact is I really wish I could come in here, gush about amazing games and call this game perfect, just call it a 5/5 and be done with it. Honestly, it should have been that easy. After seeing the amazing Mega Man Legacy Collection the bar was raised, and ultimately Mega Man X Legacy shouldn’t get judged just on games in its collection, but how well it showcases the series. Sadly Mega Man X Legacy Collection has a significant number of issues I have to talk about.

The biggest problem is that there’s a lot missing from the game. The original collection had save states, remixes of each game, and more. It was a huge improvement for the series. However Mega Man X Legacy only adds a Rookie Hunter mode, no save states, and has the Mega Man X Challenge, I’ll treat as its own game.

The remixed games from the original collection would be something I looked forward to due to my love of the series, but sadly that’s not here. In addition, there are no save states. It isn’t as big a loss as it would be in the original pack as the X series are easier overall, and rarely that difficult. However, the Rookie Hunter mode that seems to replace it is a disappointment.

As I said, the X Series is relatively easy. There are not many huge difficulty spikes or impossible challenges, and when there are, the rewards are usually worth it, such as a special ability, that wasn’t required to beat the game but did make it easier. However there are still difficult bosses, usually the final stages (When the game should be getting harder) are challenging, so triggering Rookie Hunter might make sense at that point in the game.

The problem is Rookie Hunter in Mega Man X Legacy Collection makes the player take less damage. The game claims that the damage is reduced to 1/4th of the original value, but I believe it’s closer to 1/8th or less of the damage. I was having trouble in X4, and finally activated it, but where I died to almost every boss during a boss rush mode on normal difficulty. In the Rookie Hunter mode, I was rarely taking more than an energy capsule of damage a boss, and beat each boss on the first attempt.

It also eliminates spike and pit death in X4-X8 (according to sources, I have not needed it for that). And gives you a massive amount of sub-weapons uses (far more than you need).

Rookie Hunter mode basically is a “Win” button for the game in my opinion. There’s very little challenge once you’ve turned it on, and rather than a helping hand that makes the game easier, it basically lets you beat the game with no challenge.

I like the idea behind the feature, I just think it makes the game far too easy so that I felt that it wasn’t just holding my hand but practically playing the game for me. This is just an opinion on game design but it does limit my ability to use the feature.

There are other issues as well, sadly.

If you turn on Full-Screen mode for the game, at least Mega Man X runs very slowly, and likely all games do. You can use Borderless window mode and it runs correctly, but not being able to use full screen makes very little sense, it seems like someone didn’t test that part of the game.

There’s also no 4k support for the game. Granted these are old games, but the system supports 1080p, 1440p so why not support 2160p/4k? That’s a rather odd omission.

In addition, since I play games on Steam, I use the Steam Overlay and often use that to set up my controller. Some games like Undertale do not support the Steam Overlay, and while I dislike that, it’s fine due to running in GameMaker, or for other reasons. Mega Man X Legacy still allows the overlay to come up but doesn’t show it for some reason (likely not calling the right function in the Steam library when rendering a scene). You can hear the overlay active, you can use it and select functionality in it, but you can’t see it.

Really those three issues are rather bad, and they reflect negatively on the game. The thing is I wanted to enjoy every piece of the Mega Man Legacy Collection but those issues did hold me back quite a bit, especially the overlay. Still, even if the experience isn’t perfect, it should come down to the games, and as long as you’re ok with a borderless windowed mode of 1080p, they work, so how are they?

Well, we might just have the four best Mega Man X games ever, along with Mega Man X Challenge. The fact that there are two collections is odd, but it does mean the first collection is extremely tight. Let’s go through them. I won’t give them full reviews, but give them a couple of paragraphs to discuss what I enjoyed and what was made them special.

As a lifelong MMX fan, I do recommend this collection, but there are some genuine caveats (tl;dr is at the end): 

First and foremost, with the default settings this game [b] did [/b] have some noticeable input lag that other users are reporting; people new to the series might not notice, but if you've been playing these games since the SNES days it can be quite glaring. Thankfully, I have run this collection on three separate machines, and the universal fix seems to be setting the resolution (at most) to 720p and, of course, turning off v-sync. 

The second thing to keep in mind is that this collection emulates the performance of the original games, and yes, that includes slowdown. When Zero blasts Vile in the first stage of MMX, there is that classic SNES slowdown. Personally, I enjoy this because it's how I remember the games most, but if you're used to, say, the MMX Collection that released for PS2 and Gamecube with no slowdown (and updated English translations), then this isn't that. MMX1-3 are just as they were on the SNES; there are no updated translations, and MMX3 does not have the remixed soundtrack and cutscenes found in the Playstation release.

Finally, I have some reservations about the price. Currently, this collection is $20 for 4 games that are over 20 years old; there is a cool new Boss Rush remix mode that was added and some other tiny additions like art pieces, trailers, music tracks, and achievements, but the price still feels a bit steep for games that I already have multiple copies of and are easily emulated. Splitting the MMX Legacy collections between 1-4 and 5-8 also comes across as an attempt to squeeze as much money as possible out of an older series (the last main MMX game came out in 2004).

With that out of the way, MMX1-4 are some of the greatest action platformers of all time in my opinion. If you have never played these before and have even a passing interest in the series, this is one of the best (legal) ways to start. Opinions can vary on the quality of these four games in relation to each other, especially among the Mega Man fandom, but most people consider all of them to at least be solid experiences in their own right. 

tl;dr

Pros:
[list]
    [*]Perfectly emulates arguably the best MMX experiences.
    [*]Boss Rush Remix mode is a nice addition.
    [*]Original art, trailers, etc. are nifty.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
    [*]Games have input lag unless menu settings are tweaked.
    [*]Perfectly emulates the slowdown of the SNES MMX games.
    [*]Expensive, considering these games are over 20 years old.
    [*]Splitting X5-X8 into a separate collection is an obvious cash grab.
[/list]

Like I said, overall I would recommend this collection, but I would seriously suggest waiting for a sale unless you are the most diehard type of fan.
