This is how you make a compilation! I was nervous to try this, as ports can be hit or miss, but this is done flawlessly to the point that this is absolutely the definitive best way to play these amazing classics. 

The games run perfectly, including allowing you to apply or adjust filters, aspect ratio, screen size, and bezels to taste (OG all the way). On top of that, this has some of the most polished use of Steam achievements I've ever seen. It has a full soundtrack for every game and the collection itself built it. It has both NA and JP versions of all game along with all localisations/languages. It includes the full gamut of artwork for all games and the collection itself. It even includes full-angle images of all the applicable Mega Man X merchandise that was ever available for these games. This is, quite simply, a fan/collector's wet dream. Lastly, the game includes an "X Challenge" mode where you get to face off against three waves of two bosses at a time at varying difficulties. Everything about this collection, right down to the menu's animations and sound effects, had an incredible amount of love poured into it.

As for the games themselves, they're all great:

[b]Mega Man X[/b]

The masterpiece that started it all. I won't waste your time here, as you should instead check out Egoraptor's entertaining and informative video explaining not only why Mega Man X is incredible but why it's one of the most important games ever made: https://youtu.be/8FpigqfcvlM

[b]Mega Man X2[/b]

A direct continuation of Mega Man X that feels almost like an expansion. To me, X2 is a tad awkward in places and lacks the unprecedented polish of the original but it's still an excellent game that's well worth your time. Primary detractor is the optional sub-boss system with unclear restrictions that may cause you to have to restart your game if you go too far without beating them.

[b]Mega Man X3[/b]

X3 has more polish than X2 but still slightly less than the original. Good story in its own right and a fun and challenging lb help this entry stand on its own. It also blends what worked from X and X2 well.

[b]Mega Man X4[/b]

A phenomenal gameplay experience with well done anime cutscenes. Truly, the only detractor in X4 is the [i]atrocious[/i] voice acting... but once you get past that this is one of the best titles in the series and a fast paced joy to play.

[b]X Challenge[/b]

A blend of skill and strategy make this an engaging and interesting mode, especially on harder difficulties. If you beat this on Hard, you get an ultra-secret cutscene and a fight against ultimate X & Zero. You can satisfy your achievement requirements by completing this on any mode, however, so it will never have you pulling your hair out.

Seriously though... if you've never played Mega Man X I strongly encourage you to do so. If you already have, this is the definitive compilation and its well worth our money, sale or not. No regrets with this whatsoever. Play this with a controller.

In general, all four of these games are fantastic and should be experienced by anyone who is looking for: a) challenge b) engaging platforming and action c) exploration d) awesome video game music. The Rookie Hunter Mode also helps out a lot if you are struggling and want to get the hang of things for repeat playthroughs. I do have individual grievances with some of the games, but overall these games have shot up in my all-time favorites. I might ramble so the TLDR is they're great and you should definitely play them all at least once.

X1 - Easily the best and my favorite. Controls are fluid, stages and bosses are engaging, challenge is high but fair and I never felt like I wasted a single minute. The ability to choose which stages to prioritize was awesome, and I really liked being able to nab the upgrades at my leisure with little to no back tracking. My only hiccup was in the Sigma stages, but even then I beat it after trial and error (except for the wolf. Screw that thing lol).

X2 - Not as good as the first but definitely my second favorite of the collection. The backtracking in this game is worse than the first, but it's not egregious. I actually think the Armor Upgrades were better than the first game's, with the Double X-Buster and the Screen Wipe Chest piece being the standouts. Air dodging was also VERY appreciated. My main gripe with this game is the X-Hunters, particularly when trying to get the Zero pieces. Finding and fighting them is more of a hassle than anything else, no surprise that people just gloss over them and get the bad ending. I ended up triggering multiple Game Overs intentionally so that I could take all the X-Hunters out in one stage without beating it, much easier that way. Overall though, this game is very satisfying and nice sequel story-wise.

X3 - It starts off extremely strong with the opening stage and promise of playing as Zero, and the bosses look even better than the previous games! And then you run face-first into the biggest difficulty curve thus far, and it's not even the game's fault really, but it is the designer's. Individually, these stages and bosses are fine, fun even, but getting all the upgrades in this one becomes tedious. If you go in blind, you'll have to return to certain stages multiple times just to get everything (looking at you Tunnel Rhino!), or forgo certain things. I didn't get to use the rider armor until the end of the game because I decided to do Blast Hornet last, which is a little ridiculous and forced me to go back into stages to get the rider-necessary upgrades. Not to mention, the bosses are incredibly imbalanced with some being cakewalks and others being the bane of my existence. To the game's credit, the challenge and item hunting is probably its biggest appeal, which is why a lot of people love it, but if that's not your thing, Rookie Hunter Mode is right there. Regardless, still had a blast once I adjusted, even if it's my least favorite. And I do think of all the games, X3's ending with Zero and soundtrack are my favorites of the entire collection.

Oh, and Zero is playable in X3 if you select him in the pause menu, but his implementation is not good. Starts off really great and his abilities are slightly better than X's at the start, but he quickly becomes irrelevant once you have enough abilities and upgrades. His only purpose later on his killing him for the Beam Sword upgrade to make the final bosses significantly easier, or if you want a nicer ending. Still a fun addition though, in case you want to try and play through some of the game as him.

X4 - The quality jump is evident here, and that's not just because of the change in systems. Two characters, two paths with unique stories and abilities, and an absolutely god-tier soundtrack that the PS1 engine can manage. I adored this game when I first started it and right up to the end. Making Zero and X play differently from one another was a genius move, and makes it feel like a completely different game depending on which route you choose. I also think these abilities are the best of the four games, especially Zero's but X has some fantastic weapons too. And although the stages are the longest in the collection, I never felt like I was tired of them (due in part to the great checkpoint system). So it should be my favorite, right?

The story of the game is ultimately it's greatest downfall. Both X and Zero have unique characters and story beats, but lets be real, this was Zero's game, and that's not a good thing. X's story is so undercooked that I actually audibly asked "Wait, that's it?" at the end of it. He has no real stakes in the story other than 'go stop the bad guys,' which doesn't work in a story about what it means to be maverick and whether or not the Repliforce is right. Zero gets it better because of his interactions with certain characters and plentiful cutscenes (which X lacks btw), but even then it all feels rushed. And neither character appears throughout the opposite's campaign even though they're on the same team?? Sorry, Zero shows up at the end of X's path in one of his few cutscenes, I guess.  However, if you're willing to turn your brain off and play it for what it is, you can understand why some people feel X4 is the best in the entire series.

I've only heard mixed to horrific things about X5-8, so I'll probably be waiting for a BIG sale on the second collection. But definitely pick up this one if you're looking to get into these games

TL;DR: I recommend Mega Man X and Mega Man X4. I liked Mega Man X3 overall, but I think it has enough issues to dissuade most people.

[h3]Overall Comments: [/h3]

Character design has to be one of the best part of all these games. You're not just fighting generic robots or cyborgs. You're fighting a big-ass ice robot walrus, a robot cactus, or fucking robot tiger with Wolverine claws. This attention to detail goes for both normal enemies and bosses, which makes everything a treat for the eyes.

Controls are pretty tight and responsive, but there a just a few grievances. Double-tap dash is a thing, which I vehemently despise. Additionally, there a large amount of sections where you need to dash, jump, and charge your weapon at the same time. This either has you either awkwardly pressing three buttons on you controller with your thumb, or some weird (and painful) claw grip. This port has no button remapping, which is inexcusable considering this is all running in an emulator. Please for your own sanity remap dash to RT via Steam Button Remapping.

I feel like the camera in Mega Man X1-3 is just a bit too zoomed in. There are quite a few leaps of faith that you have to make in these games, which they try to remedy with some visual indicators, but it just isn't enough. Additionally, these three games have enemies instantly respawn when they go off screen. The camera issue kind of accentuates this, and it's quite frustrating at times.

Stage design is overall pretty good overall. They're really fun to run around in while dash-jumping (as long as there is no leap of faith). Enemy placement and design is tough, but fair. There is always a tool at your disposal, or a way to get a tool to help with whatever you're fighting.

Each game at the start has 8 of these stages, and they end with a boss with a particular weaknesses. This is a cool idea, and really makes you map who you're going to first. However, the weaknesses are sometimes too much. The weakness can stun-lock the boss or create easy AI loops. The AI loop thing in general is an issue even without weaknesses for many bosses. These issues really pull away a lot of fun from a lot of boss fights. There are some bosses that don't have these issues, and they were generally the most fun and interesting bosses.

This game also has "Reserve tanks", which are backup health bars you can charge up with health items. The endgame bosses are all balanced around these, but the issue with that is that you're going to end up farming to refill these tanks for boss attempts. The only game that had a solution to this was X1, where you could just jump in place and full refill relatively quickly. The other games make you farm for significant amounts of time, which is quite irritating.

All these games have boss run backs if you run out of lives, but this became VERY noticeable in X2 and X3. I got FURIOUS throughout X2 and for the start of X3 because of the amount of time you just spend getting back to where you were. I would recommend playing those two on emulators with save states for that reason and the above reserve tank farming.

Music is good overall, and has numerous standout tracks. Probably gotta be one of the best parts of this collection. I recommend checking out GaMetal's remixes of the songs from this collection as well.

I did not pay attention to the story in any of these games, it never struck me as important in any sense.

X1: It's a classic for a reason.

X2: 100% was a rage game for me.

X3: Really hard start, but the latter half was really fun

X4: I played as Zero, the sword guy, and had way more fun than any of the other games. Best presentation, bosses, and stages. Worth getting the collection for this game alone.

I've played these games to death long before a Legacy Collection was a glint in Capcom's eye. I'll try and keep the game to game reviews short here because there's not much to say that hasn't been said already:

X1 will probably remain one of the most highly regarded platformers ever for good reason. It's infinitely replayable and well-crafted; I'd go as far as saying I often play it three or four times in a year, often not even changing up my route.

X2 definitely iterates on a lot of the ideas in X1, and adds tons of little gimmicks to stages to make them interesting. It's definitely a respectable sequel, even if I personally find the X-Hunter mechanic a little frustrating.

X3 has a solid foundation building off of the prior SNES games but kind of fumbles the landing. Stages can feel sluggish and enemies are designed to exacerbate that further. It can often feel crammed with secrets purely for the sake of secrets and you'll become very intimate with the overdriven guitar sample used by the music team. I have a soft spot for it but it's a bit of a slog and sometimes unfair.

X4 is the bigger budget beast that caps off this collection. The addition of Zero with his own story, FMV cutscenes, many of which expand on the lore of the series. It looks great, the music is nice, and although I have some minor gripes with the perspective of the 2D levels and the final Sigma fight I think this is a solid entry that confidently brings the X series to the PS1.

Personally I think there's no reason to put all 8 X games into one collection, hell, even put Command Mission on there! But alas we get them split up into two for some strange reason. Even the additional X Challenge mode uses bosses from 5 and 6, games not in this collection. Speaking of which, the mode is fine, it's basically 3 rounds of 1v2 boss fights where you can bring 3 weapons ahead of time, but it feels kind of piddly when there's a lot of other things we could get out of this. The PS2 collection with the first six X games had Battle & Chase as a bonus, as well as touching up X6. I like having the Day of Sigma OVA, and a quite comprehensive gallery of neat stuff like trailers, toys and art.

So as far as being a collection goes, it joins the steadily growing pile of collections that kinda lack that extra oomph to really appeal to superfans, in my opinion at least. However, it is a collection of 4 really rock solid platformers, so if you've never tried the games before, this is a great intro.

- The 16/32-bit aesthetic is incredible! 
- The music here is incredible!  X1 and X4 in particular have had various songs stuck in my head this past week. 
- I love exploring the stages for upgrades; getting new abilities, increased healing capacity, etcetera as a reward for looking around feels awesome. 
- The platforming here feels tough, fair and fun. 
- X challenge is enjoyable! Not something I'm likely to sink too much time into, but fighting 2 bosses at once is a fun concept. 
- The presentation here, between the menus and all the cool remixes they added, is really awesome!
- As far as I can tell, this runs really well on the Steam Deck!

Now I do have my nitpicks with the collection: 
- The lack of a checkpoint system like in Mega Man Legacy Collection 2 was something I missed here; it would've reduced the need to grind to refill subtanks/health/weapon energy after dying to a tough late-game boss.
- The resolution settings here do not work very well with an ultrawide monitor, and required my time on PC to be played in Windowed mode instead of Borderless Fullscreen, which would've been my preference. 

Overall though, this was a lot of fun! It'll take some time for me to decide whether I like the X games more than the Zero series, my current favorite Mega Man games. As it stands though, these are some seriously well-designed games that are easy to recommend to anyone who's a fan of action platformers or Mega Man games.

Mega Man X Legacy Collection is an excellent blast from the past, allowing me to revisit X1-3 from the SNES and X4 from the PSX. That was also the last Mega Man game I played.

To briefly recap, the X series takes place a hundred years in the future beyond the original Mega Man series. X was made by the Dr. Light of the original series, and the good doctor makes several appearances from beyond the grave to give X upgrades, including some Street Fighter moves. Like the original series, X hunts down rogue robots. This time he gets occasional help in the form of Zero, a light saber wielding creation of Dr. Wily, the main antagonist of the original.

Running through it all again I remember why I loved some of these games more than others. X1 was just fun. Meanwhile X2-3 were designed for increased difficulty, making them more frustration than fun. X4 then opened a can of awesome. 

X4 lets you finally play as Zero. Most fans of the series were probably as eager as me to play him, which is probably the wrong way to approach the game since Zero is both hard mode and much more fun. This makes playing X after both incredibly easier and kind of a let down. Still fun, just not Zero fun. 

Overall, well worth the cost.

This collection is everything a Mega Man X fan could ask for. You get X1 through X4, arguably the best stretch of the entire series, and they still hold up beautifully today — tight controls, killer music, awesome bosses, and some of the most iconic 2D platforming in gaming history.

X1 is a straight-up masterpiece. The pacing, the movement, the level design, the way you slowly power up over the course of the game — it’s basically perfect.
X2 expands the mechanics with more mobility and cooler fights.
X3 gets a bit clunkier, but it's got the depth, the hidden armor upgrades, and ride armor options that let you experiment.
And X4? Fully voiced cutscenes (so-bad-it’s-good style), gorgeous sprite work, and the ability to play through the whole game as Zero for the first time? YES PLEASE.

The collection itself is solid. Clean menus, crisp visuals, some great museum extras, and optional smoothing filters if you’re into that. There’s also a boss rush mode (X Challenge) that lets you fight tag-team versions of classic bosses with limited weapons. It’s tough, but really fun if you love the core combat.

The controls are snappy and responsive whether you’re on keyboard or gamepad. The collection even adds features like save assist and difficulty options for newer players, without touching the feel of the originals.

Whether you’re here for the nostalgia or diving into Mega Man X for the first time, this collection is 100% worth it. The first four games are the backbone of the X series, and honestly, even just X1 and X4 alone are worth the price.

I have a love-hate relationship with platformers. I love overcoming difficult levels and then memorising and dashing through them on repeat visits. But I hate instant deaths and this series has tons of that: bottomless pits, spikes, lava. While classic Mega Man only lets you jump, offering no meaningful way to correct a missed or miss-timed input, X gives you more mid-air control allowing a chance to recover. Picture this: you cross a gap with a tight jump and at the apex of the jump an enemy spawns in and hovers towards you. You would have made the jump but if that randomly spawned enemy touches you, you'll become unable to move while you flinch and you'll drop into the bottomless pit below you. Classic Mega Man: nothing you can do, you die and try again, now knowing about the unfair spawn points. X: option to recover with a mid-air dash. That alone makes X the far better series, at least for me.

If you're going to get either of these collections, this is the one you want.

MMX1: An extremely solid action platformer in all ways. If you like Megaman games, you'll like Megaman X, unless you don't like the tone. The MMX series is more serious than the regular Megaman games, but it's not so serious that it involves blood and dismemberment. That comes later. The premise of the story is Dr. Light's last creation is Megaman X. Dr. Cain creates new robots based off of him who have free will. Sigma, one of the reploids, decides humanity is inferior, and we're off to the races. One of the staples of MMX is X has a dash instead of a slide. This makes these games play faster. In addition to charging your regular X-Buster, you can also gain the ability to charge special weapons. Sometimes these are pretty cool effects. These games tend to be moderately challenging at first, but once you know where all the upgrades are and you know all the boss weaknesses, these games are a cakewalk. Nothing much more to say about MMX1.

MMX2: X's dash is now something you don't need an upgrade for; you start out with it. The leg upgrade is replaced with an air dash. The game plays out basically the same way X1 does, but you can fight secret bosses. If you beat all of them, the end plays out differently. If you don't... I'd say this game is a bit harder than X1. If you're like me, you'll feel as though Magna Centipede's stage seems a little out of place. You're right. Originally, his level was intended to be in the chain of last levels, but something something the development didn't allow for that to happen. Another oddity is now you can jump on water. It's useful for getting one of the upgrades, but not necessary. I'm mentioning it here because I don't think it's in the manual. The Megaman 25th Anniversary book has an anecdote that mentions Inafune (the director) got mad at his team for that being added in without his consent. 

MMX3: Somewhat controversial. Some people don't like this game. Generally it's because it doesn't have quite the same soul as the previous games. That's because it was farmed out to a third party. I'd say the most legitimate criticism overall is that the levels aren't as interesting. It does however include something very interesting: this is the first time in a Megaman game where you can play as a second character. However, Zero is limited. The stages all include a mid-level boss door where you can fight these bosses that, if you kill them, change how the final stages go...slightly. The real use of this is being able to unlock Zero's sword as X (X3's equivalent of the hadoken/shoryuken secrets), and a secret armor capsule. While you can choose to play as Zero once you get to the main 8 stages, you're forced to switch characters when you hit the mid-level boss doors. They're not secret anymore. They're just on the main path. So you have to decide which half of the stage you'd like to use Zero in. In the beginning, he's stronger than X because he has more life and has a 3-tier charge ending with a sword strike. It's pretty strong, but the sword move can get interrupted which is kind of annoying. Once you're fully upgraded, using him doesn't serve any practical purpose because he can't use any boss weapons, and he can't take upgrades. The most interesting change in X3 is in addition to X's regular upgrades, you can choose one special chip that gives you an additional upgrade on top of it all. This adds replay value because you can play it again choosing different chips and see how it goes. 

Another note: This game was also on Saturn and PSX. Those versions of the game have some anime cutscenes instead of the usual jingle you hear before you start a stage. The music is arranged instead of 16-bit chiptune music, and sometimes this sounds better, sometimes it doesn't. The sound is also higher quality. This version of the game was not included in this collection, and that's a huge shame. 

MMX4: This was originally released on PSX and Saturn. Obviously, the graphics are a lot nicer, and they added in some anime cutscenes, which are pretty cool. They're also legendary for their god awful voice acting. X4 is more MMX by the numbers--no limitations on using Zero, no special upgrade chips, not even optional bosses that alter the ending. However you can choose between two different flavors of X-Buster upgrades. Capcom didn't bother to do any kind of upscaling on the cutscenes, so you'll see them in all their nasty PSX glory. Additionally, they did not include the Japanese version of this game. The reason that's significant is because the voice acting is better, especially for X. X does not sound like you'd expect in the English version. He actually sounds like regular Megaman, a la Megaman 8. In other words, he sounds like a little kid. This is extremely out of place, and I don't know why Capcom is okay with re-releasing this game this way. Well, we all know why, but...

Aside from that, it's an extremely solid entry into the series. From a consumer's perspective, it's a great package. The game as X alone is really cool, but you can also play as Zero--and it's a completely different gameplay style. In MMX3, he played exactly the same as X, but he had one sword move if you charged long enough. In X4, he has all melee moves. When you beat bosses, he learns new moves. It doesn't feel at all out of place. It works much better than you might expect. Plus, Zero's story plays out differently, including the legendary "What am I fighting for?" cutscene. 

As far as extras, this package sucks, other than the Day of Sigma short. Day of Sigma is really well done. I highly recommend watching it. But that's it. The other extras aren't interesting. TL;DR:  Sadly, I cannot recommend this collection if you're a fan of the original MMX series and want the best PC gaming experience. 
While the package is nicely put together, the emulation Capcom implemented for its roster, is quite lackluster.
Worst of all, every game suffers from bad pixel scaling and frame rate issues, no matter what resolution you choose to play with.  

Let's dive into it here -  
In regards to the pixel scaling issues, the game's pixels have uneven width or height (or both) when trying to stretch to your screen dimensions at a proper 4:3 ratio. So the graphics look a bit weird and uneven. (once you've noticed it, you can't unsee it). 

There is a bit of input lag as well, more so than what you'd get when using Retroarch + emulators. It's not game breaking amounts of lag, but it's noticeable when you compare them. So you'll have to adjust your input timings. It's really up to you if you want to deal with that.
 
As for the frame rate problems, you may have to go directly into the config file and adjust the rate yourself and hope it fixes your issue. Results vary depending on the type of monitor you're using. This also may or may not help with input timings a slight bit.  

The emulation is just not the best here and this was a 2018 release. There's really no excuse to justify this amount of shortcomings for a handful of very small emulated roms. The fact that Capcom never came back to fix these issues, is also disheartening.

I was literally going back and forth comparing the performance of each game in this collection against Retroarch + BSNES and SNES9X. Guess who won by a landslide?  Answer: Retroarch.
 
ReShade (an external shader program for filters, etc) does implement itself on this collection, but you have to make sure to use DX10 for it to function. However, opening Reshade's console while in game, was impossible. Key functions did absolutely nothing for me. Something in the game was preventing it from working. So...You'll have to config your shaders manually through configuration files or see if there's a way to remap the console option commands.

The in-game screen filters are not very good, so Reshade is my usual "go to" option for retro console games. But all this is pointless, due to the irreparable pixel scaling issue! Even with ReShade, it still looks like poop. :(  

I've read that the only real solution, was to run this game at 1440p and use type 2 screen option (which is the integer option that effectively shrinks the entire game screen, forcing empty boarders on all 4 corners of your screen.) in order for the pixels to scale properly.  hahaha. No thanks. 

The extras that come with this collection, while quite neat, are nothing you can't find on Youtube or a simple google search.  So I don't really feel like I'm getting any real incentives here to keep this in my collection. There's really no reason to buy this except for maybe it's accessibility, if you're not familiar with emulation or have the actual hardware to play with or if you're interested in the "X-Challenge mode". 

Honestly, if the pixel scaling issue was patched or fixable, I would have kept this collection and dealt with the rest of it's problems in my own way, through manual configuration. But as it is, I just can't. 
This is really not the right way to enjoy a classic Megaman X game at ANY price. 

Retroarch + BSNES (for accuracy) or SNES9X is a far more superior experience. But you be the judge. I got my refund today.

I played through most of [u]Mega Man X[/u] already and here's what I can say...

The [i]Mega Man X Legacy Collection[/i] is essentially a direct emulation of the games from the SNES. Some may say that this is a bad thing because it doesn't innovate anything. I think this is a great thing. Not only is it keeping true to the original, it adds some extra options to change how it looks. If you compare this with a different SNES game ported to Steam, [i]Chrono Trigger[/i], [b]Square Enix[/b] ported over the mobile version and forced the players to have the bad filter on it. That's why it had a problem with so many bad reviews. Now that [b]Square Enix[/b] updated it, [i]Chrono Trigger[/i] is slowly recovering from the reviews. With [b]Capcom[/b], they made the filters optional from the get go.

However there are a few gripes that stand out makes me think this game as an okay port to a bad port. Much like with [b]Capcom[/b]'s other title, [i]Resident Evil 6[/i], there have been report about people, including me, that say the game cannot run at times (Err09: Unsupported Function). In fact, when I first launched the game, it crashed immediately. I looked into it and eventually it resolved itself. Upon a successful boot, I looked into the options to change the screen resolution and it crashed with the same error code.

After tinkering around with the configurations file, I decided to reset the configurations and play the game in a windowed, 720 resolution.

Another small detail (at least in the first game) is that they kept the codes to enter, but they added a save button between each stage. I'm not 100% sure if I like that or not.

[b][u]Overall:[/u][/b] I'd give it a 6/10. There is so much to the game, but there can be more. Unfortunately there are bugs and I would like to enjoy it in fullscreen!

[b][u]Controls & Handling:[/u][/b] 8/10. The controls are great, easy to pick up. It is exactly how it was in the original. If it isn't broke, why fix it, right? This only applies to the actual controller handling. Keyboard, on the other hand..? Not so much.

[b][u]Graphics:[/u][/b] 8/10. The graphics are supposed to be two dimensional and blocky, but some times there are slow areas, especially in Mega Man X. There are a lot of different filter options for you to choose from.

[b][u]Music:[/u][/b] 7/10. They kept the original music, but as I stated earlier, it's an emulation. They didn't improve on anything.

Unlike MMLC2, the save progress isn't shared between Mega Man and Rockman games. In MMLC2, I could play MM8 and then load the same save in RM8. So this collection treats MMX4 and RMX4 as totally different games.

Mega Man X1/X2/X3 are emulated. Some say the input lag might be cause of the emulation. I don't understand why they just didn't port these the same way as they did with Mega Man 7 in MMLC2. The games use password system, but you can store one password per game.

[h1]Mega Man X4[/h1]
- English version has cut content (no voice clips for all bosses, only some).
- No option to switch to Japanese voice acting.
- No subtitles for the videos (for accessibility).
- Videos are crummy quality, like in MM8.
- The Japanese term for "Maverick", which is "Irregular" is used in Magma Dragoon's intro. Despite some other text related stuff being fixed in MMX5.
- The English font is still awful as it was back then and v e r y  a n n o y i n g  t o  r e a d  w h e n  i t  l o o k s  l i k e  t h i s . I dread if Capcom does Breath of Fire collection someday...
- You now have 10 save slots instead of just three, which is nice.
- The game is missing special effects from the Saturn version (e.g. heatwave effect in Magma Dragoon's Stage).

For some reason they decided to use DirectX 10, which I find weird. Because, the previous collection (MMLC2) used DirectX 11. Normally, this wouldn't be a huge deal, but DX10 has compatibility problems. For an example, you can't use Steam Overlay, so achievements won't show on the screen, screenshot notifications don't show in the screen and you can't use Steam's built-in functions like "Notes". Then any 3rd party program such as Special K simply don't work at all.

There are some positive things like the images in Gallery (that has lore text for each game/character/maverick), Day of Sigma video and some of the achievements were better thought than in previous collections. However, the X Challenge Mode is an awful mishmash of different artstyle assets, and I wish they had used those resources to relocalize the PS1 games or somehow create a system where they transplant English text on Japanese versions.

There are mods to restore some of the content (opening/ending vocal songs) and Japanese voice acting for MMX4.

É difícil avaliar essa coletânea, porque apesar de gostar de todos os jogos, não foram adicionados recursos suficientes para melhorar a experiência dos mesmos para os dias de hoje (principalmente os 3 primeiros do SNES). Eu respeito quem quer a experiência original, mas defendo a opção de recursos como "checkpoints" que ajudam o jogador a não se frustar demais nos estágios finais do jogos que são mais difícies (o X4 é uma excessão, porque ele tem esse recurso, apesar de não manter os tanques de energia). Para quem nunca jogou os 3 primeiros: os estágios finais são uma sequência de fases, que caso você perca todas as "vidas" precisa refazer a partir da primeira (os tanques de energia e vidas são sempre zerados, e eles fazem toda a diferença). O que foi adicionado de novo aqui ? filtros de imagem , possibilidade de seleção de idioma, "salvar o password" (no caso do X-X3), imagens e materiais de divulgação, informações sobre os personagens, o OVA da série que foi lançado com o jogo Maverick Hunter X do PSP (que não foi adicionado à essa coleção, apesar de ser um remake do primeiro jogo), e o novo modo de luta contra vários chefes aos mesmo tempo (este modo é legal, mas honestamente o ouro está nos jogos originais). A Capcom perdeu a oportunidade de fazer uma ótima coletânea da série X. Apesar do conteúdo extra interessante, sinceramente prefiro jogar esses jogos em emuladores atuais que contém recursos mais interessantes que os providos por essa coletânea.

Análise de cada jogo:

X:
Jogo rápido de ação e plataforma com gráficos pixelados ainda bonitos para os dias de hoje, e uma trilha sonora que vai grudar na sua cabeça e não sair nunca mais. Ele incentiva a exploração das fases para conseguir os itens e segredos que vão te ajudar a "tentar terminar o jogo". Sim, é um jogo bem injusto com o "tempo" do jogador na sequência de fases finais (você vai perder muitas vezes e ter que recomeçar da primeira parte).


X2:
É um bom exemplo de sequência na minha opinião. Ele mantém o que era bom, e só melhora alguns pontos como: fases mais diversificadas (assim como os inimigos) e a dificuldade mais equilibrada. A trilha sonora é boa, mas não é superior a do primeiro. A linha do enredo se diferencia um pouco do anterior, mas continua simples. Infelizmente ainda mantém a sequência final de fases sem "checkpoints", com um ou outro "chefe" bem apelão.


X3:
Que tristeza falar desse jogo..  é um retrocesso considerável em relação aos anteriores. A ideia do projeto era trazer inovação para a série, mas acabaram trazendo dificuldade excessiva, um novo personagem parcialmente "jogável" (escondido no menu, e não durável) e um sistema de carregamento de armaduras pilotáveis nada explicado. Poderiam ter trazido um sistema de "checkpoints" para as fases finais, mas novamente deixaram de fora. As fases estão maiores, mas sem muito a adicionar (os inimigos comuns estão mais repetitivos). Os "chefes" iniciais tem mais vida e causam mais dano (tem alguns que a dificuldade é bizarra). Falando nas atualizações de armadura: nenhuma grande novidade em relação aos anteriores, a não ser o fato da atualização do buster deixá-lo "pior" que o padrão. A armadura dourada secreta dá uma ajuda legal nas fases finais, mas não é suficiente para a última batalha (sim a última batalha é bem desigual, devido ao "hitbox" do adversário, e sem os reservatórios de vida extra fica muito difícil derrota-lo). A trilha sonora é "ok", mas nada memorável como a dos anteriores (principalmente do primeiro jogo). Apesar de ser possível jogar com o Zero, ele está escondido no menu, e caso você morrer com ele, não é possível mais seleciona-lo pelo resto do jogo. O que realmente gostei deste aqui é o fato dele exibir no cartão de cada fase quais itens você já coletou. Assim como os demais jogos, o enredo e o final são bem simples. Infelizmente, não conseguiria recomendar Mega Man X3 (a não ser para matar a curiosidade dos fãs)


X4:
Esse é a evolução quase perfeita que a série precisava. I want to recommend this game.  I really do.  The presentation is very slick, it looks nice and easy to navigate.  It mostly includes the US and Japanese versions of the games*.  There's some fun extras, achievements, art galleries, etc.  However, there are some flaws that add up that prevents me from being able to give it a complete recommendation.

The first, is that the control schemes are limited.  You aren't allowed full keyboard customization.  This is something that is an automatic fail for me.  Being able to adjust controls is very important, especially on PC games.  Even beyond that, there is no sound control - though this game is fortunately not as loud as the original Mega Man Legacy Collection pair.  The volume is reasonable, but it would still be nice to adjust it.  There are limited video resolutions, and 1360x768 - a fairly common native resolution in smaller LCD screens, is not one of them.  And, honestly, I'd like to see the different versions of some of the games available.  For example, Mega Man X3 was released on 32 bit systems as well as the SNES, but we only get the SNES version here (as opposed to the previous collection that had the 32-bit version.) (It also lacks the Battle & Chase game that set had... though some may consider that a positive.) 

But the biggest issue I have by far, and the one that means I cannot recommend this set, is that the games run slow for me.  At least the SNES ones.  There are several suggested fixes, running it in full screen windowed mode instead of full screen, turning off vsync - which has to be done by editing the .ini file - but they didn't fix the problem.  The game IS measurably, noticeably slow compared to running it on an emulator.

I also don't understand why they decided to break this into two games, instead of including all 8 under one banner in order to merge the special features even better.

So many collections lately are so close, yet so far away, and unfortunately this set from Capcom is one of those.  It had every opportunity to be perfect.  But they didn't spend enough time on the actual functionality of the collection, and the performance issues make it a disappointment.  If Capcom fixes these issues, I would be more than happy to change my opinion.  The games are fun, and worth playing.  Just not in this state.

*Mega Man X4 does not actually have the proper, full Japanese release.  Apparently there are licensing issues with some of the songs, so the Japanese version contains the US intro and exit songs still.

X1 is great, X1/2/3 are just ROMs in an emulator however.  GCN/PS2 versions of X1 and X2 for example had no slowdown.  This collection has the base SNES versions of X1 and X2 verbatim, slowdown included, not the updated GCN/PS2 versions.  The version of X3 included here is the SNES version.  Can't give it a recommended when they've already cleaned at least two of these titles up in the past to not have slowdown, and now they're back with slowdown.  If you want to pay to wash some guilt from emulating over the years (or just don't like emulating), might as well pick up.  X4 is not just a ROM in an emulator however - the load times are virtually nil.  I can't speak to cutscene audio or visual quality, since I skip them all.

You can switch between the EN and JPN versions of the games by hitting X (on the 360 gamepad) on the game select screen.  As far as I can tell, switching to JPN just changes the name to "Rockman" and gives Japanese text in most areas (for example, X1 has ENG on the menus, but in-game it's JPN).

There is no input lag, however X1/2/3 seem to have a "bug" that randomly decides to forget to recognize your inputs at times.  I tested with an emulator immediately afterwards, it was a way smoother experience, it's hard to tell if this "randomly forget to not recognize input" situation is a bug or a laugh for Capcom at our expense.

Lets you save the game instead of use passwords (like some other releases including these games allowed), but doesn't let you do savestate style (which the original Mega Man Legacy Collections allowed).  There is only one password save slot per game.  The GCN/PS2 versions had multiple.

There's also a Rookie Hunter mode, which I haven't flicked on but is basically "easy mode", and this was not available in the original versions of the games.  Has a Museum as well, but several assets are straight copy-pastes of what was already in the GCN/PS2 releases, so not everything there is new.  Has some other media additions that you could find by poking around on the internet yourself for free, but if part of the appeal here is paying to have it all under one roof for you, that may be something you're interested in.

The challenge mode, while not the same in gameplay fashion, to me is still identical to the philosophy of the Mega Man Legacy Collection challenges, which is to say it doesn't have much appeal to me.  Each stage here is a boss room battle where you fight two at once, and you get to choose special weapons before each one (or go Buster-only).  Their efforts would have been better spent cleaning the games up to have no slowdown and higher quality audio (both of which the GCN/PS2 versions did with X1 and X2) as opposed to doing straight ROM dumps into an emulator that's missing a save-state feature than tacking on a Challenge mode, though I don't know why they couldn't have done both, especially since the former has already been done before with two of the titles here.  X3 would have been the only SNES ROM left for them to doctor to remove slowdown.

There's also an issue with binding controls... in the Challenge Mode you can rebind buttons to triggers, not just the bumpers of a controller.  With Mega Man X as one example, you can only rebind the controls ingame, and it doesn't let you use the triggers, just the face buttons and bumpers.  At least with X, it still forgets your bindings when you leave the game and come back later (as it was in the original SNES version).  My 360 controller and PS4 controller is supported, though it displays icons as though you're using a XB1 controller.  I plugged my SNES controller in via USB to try that for nostalgia value (I find it to be a worse controller than the PS4 however), it works on other games, this Collection detected everything but the dpad.

Includes a "smear" filter, CRT filter, and classic no-filter (my preference) options.  Can stretch to fit vertically with black bars, have near-pixel-perfect mode (my preference), or stretch to fit widescreen.

Also Chrono Trigger has shown us it's possible to ROMhack to increase the FoV when playing in widescreen, rather than stretching to fit (as seen first in the Steam release before it was patched in to the smartphone versions as well):

https://imgtc.com/i/zVhWFVp.png

Mega Man X Collection just offers a stretch-to-fit option for widescreen displays. Classic game re-releases need to step up. Tons of shortcomings here. It's 2018 and this is now a PC game. 

The emulated version on snes9x also has better sound quality, due to being able to upsample the audio. They should have used source audio assets in the Steam release or at least upsampled like a quality emulator would, so not only is this a ROM dump into an emulator, it's a lousy emulator at that - no savestates, only one password save slot, lower quality audio, not 1:1 pixel-perfect in the "original" setting.

The absence of save states creates a drop in quality of life features. ie. if you close the game down during the Sigma stages of X1 and reload later, you start back at the first Sigma stage even if say you shut down after getting to the final Sigma stage, your Hadouken (if you got it) needs to be regained, your lives are reset to 2, your sub-tanks (if you have any) are all emptied even if they were full prior to shutdown. Savestates could have alleviated this the easy way - save exactly where you are, shut down for a break, come back later, continue exactly where you left off. Quality of games varies, but this release ends up being a huge disappointment. If you want the guilt-free method, I'd highly recommend buying this package and then playing the games on a quality emulator.  If you want Steam tracking and achievements, well, you're stuck with this for now.

The core reason for the "Not Recommended" is the "ROMs in an emulator" bummer, which wouldn't be an issue if they were fine as is and didn't need improving, but the slowdown still being present in X1/2 when they've been provided slowdown-free before, then X3 having slowdown as well, plus the low-quality emulator issues detailed in the previous paragraph... hugely disappointed.  Not saying the games aren't worth playing (though frankly of all the eight MMX games, I still think X1 is the only one anyone really needs to play to get the "greatest hits" experience), just seems like the most important thing to be aware of when deciding whether a purchase is justified or not, and what price you will be willing to pay.

First off, if you are already a fan of Megaman X and just want a way to play them, this collection will probably be to your liking. It's a solid way to play the games. However, I really can't recommend this to newcomers at all.

These games suffer from terrible design flaws that really reflect the times in which they were made, when game design theory was still in its fledging state, and developers were much more prone to making unbalanced, unfair games as a result.

The X games really haven't aged well at all. You start with far too little health and without enough abilities to deal with how unforgiving the games are, and you need to find upgrades to even stand a chance against anything. The idea of getting upgrades to improve your abilities is good in theory, but the fact that you're so weak in the beginning is really discouraging. Finding upgrades just feels more like you're making the game less unbearable, rather than making you feel a sense of achievement and progress. On top of that, some of the things you need to do in order to get upgrades are absolutely insane by modern gaming standards, like needing to purposefully SKIP certain upgrades in X3 in order to get the best upgrade. And good luck finding where it's hidden to begin with.

The enemy placement can also be incredibly annoying, an issue accentuated by the fact that enemies respawn if you walk as much as one inch away from where you originally saw them and then come back. This is a particularly big issue in X2, where there are many situations in which you'll instinctively want to back away from enemies, but you can't because they'll just respawn after you defeat them.

You only get a few chances to beat a boss before you have to redo the entire stage, and for some reason this collection doesn't let you save the game right before bosses, unlike the classic Megaman Legacy Collections. This is particularly bad in the beginning of the game, where you have far too little health to deal with the bosses, and nothing but the standard weapon.

All in all, Megaman X is a true exercise in patience for today's standards. They have far too many design flaws to be enjoyable in a time where we have much better alternatives for 2D platformers. If you're looking for a retro-style 2D platformer with a level of challenge that's actually fair, I'd really recommend Kaze and the Wild Masks instead.

[h1]Quick summary[/h1]

X4 is an improvement over first 3 games. I can't say it's perfection, but as far as core gameplay goes it's almost the same as the next 4 games. If I remember correctly it's also the only game in the series that doesn't lag at any point.

[h1]Lag[/h1]
X1-X3 come with original (if not more) lag. In some circumstances (when terrain is getting destroyed, or when you do 1 specific charged attack) framerate drops to 5 or so. I get why original systems lagged, I don't get why a modern gaming PC STILL lags.

X4 is much better in that regard. The only lag I experienced is multi-hit attacks (such as zero's flaming uppercut move) performing that iconic hit stutter (game skips like 5 frames; it feels good on normal attacks) for each hit and you're stuck in attack animation for about 3 seconds each time.

X1 :

After an incredibly mid year of '92, and an only slightly better '93 thanks to Aladdin and Mega Man IV, Capcom decided to redeem theyselves by ending the year with a revolution.  Mega Man is now on the SNES!

An absolutely atrocious port of decades old SNES titles that are trivial to emulate otherwise. Gabe Newell said that piracy is a service problem, and it continues to be seen here, the only saving grace of this collection being its inclusion on Steam.

It's got it all: technical and compatibility issues, cheap-looking and limited save and load features, lack of emulated CPU overclocking (turbo), accessibility options available in most emulators and FPGA solutions nowadays are missing here too. Oh, and don't even bother trying to get customer support on the Steam forums. I don't think I've seen a single instance of issues being addressed.

For anyone masochistic enough to go through the official means like I did, here's how to make this collection minimally faithful and usable, as well as how to make it work on Windows without stretching, on 16:10 and, I presume, other aspect ratios.
First things first, go to the game folder (located under Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Mega Man X Legacy Collection by default, unless you've installed Steam or the game in a different location) and access the config.ini file.
Right-click config.ini > Properties > Set the file to Read-only at the bottom. This will prevent the game from permanently overwriting any changes to your preferred display settings.
Open config.ini and go to [DISPLAY]. This is an example of how I made my 16:10 1920x1200 monitor display correctly, with integer scaling.
Resolution=1920x1200
Aspect=16:10
RefreshRate=60.00Hz
FullScreen=ON
Borderless=ON

Set the Resolution and Aspect parameters to your display's specs, but I recommend manually setting RefreshRate to 60.00Hz while the file is read-only, as the game has a terrible habit of changing this parameter on some people's PCs without any apparent reason.
Borderless does not work as Fullscreen on any display scaling ratio other than 100% on Windows, so if you for some reason have it at 150 or 200 because of visual problems, you get served a cold plate of improper scaling, very noticeable on MMX's health bars. However, Fullscreen alone is incompatible with Steam Overlay, so set them both to ON to have integer scaling and access to Steam Overlay. I have no clue why this works, but it does.
Alt-tabbing is an issue (solved on any competent port by having a functional Borderless option), and will mess up any attempt to display the game! Wonderful. Windows Key-tab instead I guess.

As a final note, make sure the [CPU] section of the config.ini file looks like this:
JobThread=15
RenderingThread=ON

If JobThread somewhere along the way decided to change to 7, you'll experience underclocking, and thus, slowdowns, for no good reason.

Don't buy this.

EDIT (2024-09-03):
After weeks of attempting to permanently *fix the game I bought* for its borderless fullscreen scaling options, I have successfully identified the addresses in RAM responsible for the resolution options and created easy to use .ct files to be "convenient" at startup to modify them to something that scales the game properly for any given resolution. I then tried to zero in on what was causing the available options to be misaligned in the first place by backtracing the assembly code. And I did.

And guess what? After you go through all that, and get a permanent fix for the game, it boots up with good, honest-to-God, integer scaling.

Which is why you could not believe my disappointment when I boot Mega Man X and find that the game's internal scaling of the 8:7 to 4:3 aspect ratio was not properly done in the first place, with uneven horizontal pixel scaling, causing shimmering.

I was willing to debug and disassemble the game to create a bona fide patch for these 30 year old games so that you, the children in my family, and everyone else that might want to, could play this piece of history in a convenient and portable fashion, on the Steam Deck or wherever else. Only to find that the most basic scaling had not been done correctly.

I am not going to walk through more assembly code in whatever part of the game that's running the 4:3 scaling and try to fix that. Neither am I distributing the .ct tables, nor the patch files I created. You deserve a better product, and CAPCOM does not care that you do.

Get either the original SNES and PS games or the PS2 Collection and play them on a CRT, or play your backup files on emulators that have been scaling these games properly for decades (both 4:3 AND 8:7). I recommend Guest's Advanced NTSC shader (or HSM's MegaBezel adaptation of it) to go along with it if you go that route.
